Description: German Clickworker respondents (n=993, March 2019) chose which of two MPs running for re-election they would vote for, in 5 tasks; profiles varied the MP's knowledge focus (constituency/national/European), reason for absences, effort on Eurozone reform, gender, motivation, years in parliament and party (German text).
Reference: Senninger, R., & Bischof, D. (2023). Do voters want domestic politicians to scrutinize the European Union? Political Science Research and Methods, 11(2), 410-418.
Notes: data/conjoint/senninger_2023.R. AfD profiles always 'zwei Jahren' in parliament. trial_block_order = survey questions before/after the conjoint. Covariates are German answer text. dataframe12.RData in the deposit holds Qualtrics ResponseIds (column IPAddress), not used.

Description: 998 US YouGov respondents each chose between 2 restaurants in 5 tasks; restaurants varied in distance, price, online reviews, a hiring initiative (more employees, LGBTQ people, people with a criminal conviction record, veterans) and staff racial composition. Outcome is the preferred restaurant.
Reference: Shi, L., & Denver, M. (2025). The transferal of criminal record stigma in the employment context: Evidence from conjoint and vignette experiments. Criminology, 63(1), 89-121.
Notes: data/conjoint/shi_2025.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (one preferred per consecutive pair). Level text from .dta value labels; the Data Dictionary reverses the staff codes and says 'Terrible' for 'Negative' (the .dta labels kept, supported by respondent-race pattern). Vignette experiment in the same deposit not built.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n=747, May 2022) chose which of two hypothetical student-loan borrowers (occupation, race, employment, college type, debt level, amount owed, time in repayment, repayment history) most deserves debt forgiveness, and rated each 1-5 on deservingness; 4 pairs each are kept (tasks 5-6, where race is not recorded, are dropped).
Reference: SoRelle, M. E., & Laws, S. (2024). Deservingness and the politics of student debt relief. Perspectives on Politics, 22(2), 372-390.
Notes: data/conjoint/sorelle_2024.R. Race only in tasks 1-4 (absent from the deposit for tasks 5-6; authors analyse tasks 1-4). Authors' do-file assigns borrower A's repayment history to borrower B; table uses the correct column. The deposit's second (relief-plan) conjoint has no attributes and is not built.

Description: Face-to-face national sample in Costa Rica (n = 818; 820 fielded, 2013-14) chose between pairs of hypothetical partner countries for a trade agreement, described by 8 attributes (economic size, culture, distance, religion, political system, environmental and labour standards, military alliance), and rated support for each (1-7).
Reference: Spilker, G., Bernauer, T., & Umaña, V. (2016). Selecting partner countries for preferential trade agreements: Experimental evidence from Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Vietnam. International Studies Quarterly, 60(4), 706-718.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/spilker_2016.R. Level text = authors' English figure labels (respondents saw Spanish). Economic size from the authors' dummies (Costa Rica value label reversed). 266 tasks dropped (political system missing in 311 rows; 13 tasks with no choice). Same survey as spilker_2018_trade_costa_rica (different experiment). Vietnam not built (alliance coding contradictory).

Description: Face-to-face national sample in Nicaragua (n = 789; 800 fielded, 2013-14) chose between pairs of hypothetical partner countries for a trade agreement, described by 8 attributes (economic size, culture, distance, religion, political system, environmental and labour standards, military alliance), and rated support for each (1-7).
Reference: Spilker, G., Bernauer, T., & Umaña, V. (2016). Selecting partner countries for preferential trade agreements: Experimental evidence from Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Vietnam. International Studies Quarterly, 60(4), 706-718.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/spilker_2016.R. Level text = authors' English figure labels (respondents saw Spanish). Economic size from the authors' dummies (Costa Rica value label reversed). 786 tasks dropped (economic size missing for task 5 profile 1 of 536 respondents; political system missing in 335 rows). Same survey as spilker_2018_trade_nicaragua (different experiment). Vietnam not built (alliance coding contradictory).

Description: District-choice conjoint: 1,200 Afro-Colombian adults (online convenience sample, Oct-Nov 2021) each chose which of two hypothetical electoral districts (ethnic reserved-seat vs territorial, number of candidates, experience, vote buying, candidates' ethnicity, past projects, networks) they would vote in, 3 times; forced choice.
Reference: Villamizar-Chaparro, M., & Echeverri-Pineda, C. (2025). Group consciousness, organizational membership, and district choice: Evidence from the Afro-Colombian reserved seats. Political Behavior, 47, 825-846.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/villamizar_2024.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (exactly one chosen per pair). Display language not documented (presumably Spanish); attr_ text is the authors' short English labels from the deposit, which differ in places from the article's Table 1 (Networks level 'No community or family' vs 'Both family and the community'; 'More than 14' vs 'More than 15').

Description: Candidate choice conjoint fielded online in Poland (2021): respondents compared 12 pairs of hypothetical Sejm candidates differing in party, policy and stances on judicial appointments and public media (2,909 respondents). Outcomes: vote choice and a 1-7 approval rating of each candidate.
Reference: Wunsch, N., Jacob, M. S., & Derksen, L. (2025). The demand side of democratic backsliding: How divergent understandings of democracy shape political choice. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e39.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wunsch_2025.R. Respondents saw Polish; attr_ text is the authors' English (SI Table A.1). All 2,909 respondents kept with the authors' attention-check flags (analytic sample 1,979). Hungary replication file not built (re-hosted subset of another study).

Description: US respondents (n=1,080) saw 6 pairs of hypothetical immigrant profiles (age, years in the U.S., gender, race, English, education, police record, benefits) and picked the one they thought was the 'illegal' or the 'undocumented' immigrant, the term randomized between respondents (trial_condition).
Reference: Zhirkov, K., & Brehm, R. H. (2025). Beliefs and opinions about "illegal" and "undocumented" immigrants: Conceptual replication of a null result. Research & Politics, 12(3).
Notes: data/conjoint/zhirkov_2025_illegal.R. Attribute text from the authors' Stata value labels (displayed wording may be longer); question wording not deposited; 40 tasks with no chosen profile dropped (3 respondents entirely). Article not read (publisher blocks access).

Description: US Lucid respondents (n=1,964, August 2022) rated 30 single profiles of a person (race, gender, marital status, children, immigration status, employment status, criminal record) on how typical each is of welfare recipients, 0-10. The article analyses the 1,271 non-Hispanic white respondents with varying ratings.
Reference: Zhirkov, K., Lunz Trujillo, K., & Myers, C. D. (2025). Measuring support for welfare policies: Implications for the effects of race and deservingness stereotypes. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12(1), 126-133.
Notes: data/conjoint/zhirkov_2025.R. All 1,964 respondents kept; article sample (cov_ethnicity==1 & cov_hispanic==1 & non-constant ratings) = 1,271, reproduced along with the Figure A2 AMCEs. Rating question wording is the article's paraphrase (export text truncated); scale end labels not deposited.

Description: Argentine respondents (Respondi quota sample, February 2020; 1,688 respondents, 1,527 in the author's sample) chose which of two hypothetical individuals should pay a higher tax rate, over 5 pairs varying annual income, share of income paid in sales taxes and source of income (effort, family connections, government bailout, lottery).
Reference: Alvarado, M. (2024). Compensation and tax fairness: Evidence from four countries. British Journal of Political Science, 54(4), 1023-1042.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/alvarado_2024.R (one script, four country tables; level text differs by country and language). choice = 1 for the person chosen to pay more tax. cov_in_authors_sample reproduces the article's N (1,527). Raw export carried IP, geolocation, postcode and free-text justifications (dropped).

Description: Australian respondents (Respondi quota sample, February 2020; 1,633 respondents, 1,450 in the author's sample) chose which of two hypothetical individuals should pay a higher tax rate, over 5 pairs varying annual income, share of income paid in sales taxes and source of income (effort, family connections, government bailout, lottery).
Reference: Alvarado, M. (2024). Compensation and tax fairness: Evidence from four countries. British Journal of Political Science, 54(4), 1023-1042.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/alvarado_2024.R (one script, four country tables; level text differs by country and language). choice = 1 for the person chosen to pay more tax. cov_in_authors_sample reproduces the article's N (1,450). Raw export carried IP, geolocation, postcode and free-text justifications (dropped).

Description: Chilean respondents (Respondi quota sample, February 2020; 1,584 respondents, 1,418 in the author's sample) chose which of two hypothetical individuals should pay a higher tax rate, over 5 pairs varying annual income, share of income paid in sales taxes and source of income (effort, family connections, government bailout, lottery).
Reference: Alvarado, M. (2024). Compensation and tax fairness: Evidence from four countries. British Journal of Political Science, 54(4), 1023-1042.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/alvarado_2024.R (one script, four country tables; level text differs by country and language). choice = 1 for the person chosen to pay more tax. cov_in_authors_sample reproduces the article's N (1,418). Raw export carried IP, geolocation, postcode and free-text justifications (dropped).

Description: US respondents (Amazon Mechanical Turk, October 2017; 2,081 respondents, 1,946 in the author's sample) chose which of two hypothetical individuals should pay a higher tax rate, over 5 pairs varying annual income, share of income paid in sales taxes and source of income (effort, family connections, government bailout, lottery).
Reference: Alvarado, M. (2024). Compensation and tax fairness: Evidence from four countries. British Journal of Political Science, 54(4), 1023-1042.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/alvarado_2024.R (one script, four country tables; level text differs by country and language). choice = 1 for the person chosen to pay more tax. cov_in_authors_sample reproduces the article's N (1,946). The author's US entropy-balancing weights are not deposited. Raw export carried IP, geolocation, postcode and free-text justifications (dropped).

Description: Climate-agreement conjoint: 2,000 adults in Germany (YouGov internet sample, summer 2012) each compared 4 pairs of hypothetical global climate agreements varying household cost, cost distribution, participating countries, emissions covered, sanctions and monitoring body; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-10 referendum vote rating.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Scheve, K. F. (2013). Mass support for global climate agreements depends on institutional design. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110(34), 13763-13768.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2013.R (one of four country tables; the article pools them, but costs and sanctions were shown in local currency amounts). Respondents saw German; attr_ text is English from the article's Table 1 and SI, with this country's amounts. Profile position inferred from row order. Same data re-hosted in Ratkovic & Tingley's archive doi:10.7910/DVN/RNMB1Q.

Description: Climate-agreement conjoint: 2,000 adults in France (YouGov internet sample, summer 2012) each compared 4 pairs of hypothetical global climate agreements varying household cost, cost distribution, participating countries, emissions covered, sanctions and monitoring body; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-10 referendum vote rating.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Scheve, K. F. (2013). Mass support for global climate agreements depends on institutional design. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110(34), 13763-13768.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2013.R (one of four country tables; the article pools them, but costs and sanctions were shown in local currency amounts). Respondents saw French; attr_ text is English from the article's Table 1 and SI, with this country's amounts. Profile position inferred from row order. Same data re-hosted in Ratkovic & Tingley's archive doi:10.7910/DVN/RNMB1Q.

Description: Climate-agreement conjoint: 2,000 adults in United Kingdom (YouGov internet sample, summer 2012) each compared 4 pairs of hypothetical global climate agreements varying household cost, cost distribution, participating countries, emissions covered, sanctions and monitoring body; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-10 referendum vote rating.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Scheve, K. F. (2013). Mass support for global climate agreements depends on institutional design. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110(34), 13763-13768.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2013.R (one of four country tables; the article pools them, but costs and sanctions were shown in local currency amounts). Respondents saw English; attr_ text is English from the article's Table 1 and SI, with this country's amounts. Profile position inferred from row order. Same data re-hosted in Ratkovic & Tingley's archive doi:10.7910/DVN/RNMB1Q.

Description: Climate-agreement conjoint: 2,500 adults in United States (YouGov internet sample, summer 2012) each compared 4 pairs of hypothetical global climate agreements varying household cost, cost distribution, participating countries, emissions covered, sanctions and monitoring body; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-10 referendum vote rating.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Scheve, K. F. (2013). Mass support for global climate agreements depends on institutional design. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110(34), 13763-13768.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2013.R (one of four country tables; the article pools them, but costs and sanctions were shown in local currency amounts). Respondents saw English; attr_ text is English from the article's Table 1 and SI, with this country's amounts. Profile position inferred from row order. Same data re-hosted in Ratkovic & Tingley's archive doi:10.7910/DVN/RNMB1Q.

Description: 1,004 US MTurk respondents each chose between 4 pairs of hypothetical House primary candidates in their own party's primary, described by job, office experience, polling, and four campaign-message statements (pluralism/people-centrism, moralism/anti-establishment, immigration, economy).
Reference: Dai, Y., & Kustov, A. (2024). The (in)effectiveness of populist rhetoric: A conjoint experiment of campaign messaging. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(4), 849-856.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dai_2024.R. Level text is the deposit's displayed statements (match online appendix Table B1 up to contractions); the authors' populism/congruence codings are dropped (rebuild from the statement lists in Table B1). Derived populist-attitude flags dropped. cov_attention_pass marks the ~70% who passed the attention check.

Description: 2,397 Black, White and mixed Black-White US adults (Qualtrics Panels, Dec 2020-Feb 2021) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical people varying parents' race (in half the forms), gender, skin tone, class, neighborhood, spouse, incarceration, discrimination and party; they picked the person who is more Black and rated each 0-10 on how Black.
Reference: Davenport, L. D., Jefferson, H., & Rendleman, H. E. (2026). The politics of Black classification: Sociopolitical cues and racial perception. Perspectives on Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/davenport_2026.R. Four randomized forms pooled (ancestry shown or not; skin-tone row top or bottom) as trial_ columns; attr_parents blank when not shown. The per-profile 'how does this person identify' answer (Black/Mixed race/White) is not stored. Article DOI not known at build; Qualtrics ids re-keyed.

Description: Dynata online samples in Brazil, Germany, South Africa and the US (Aug-Sep 2023, n=12,059) compared 3 pairs of proposals for a new global organization on energy production and consumption, varying whether companies, scientists, civil-society organizations and individual energy consumers get a lot of say; they chose the most appropriate proposal and rated confidence in the organization (1-7).
Reference: Ecker-Ehrhardt, M., Verhaegen, S., & Quack, S. (2025). Nonstate actor inclusion and the social legitimacy of global governance institutions. International Studies Quarterly, 69(2), sqaf040.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/eckerehrhardt_2025.R. One of two experiments done by the same respondents (energy and internet tables share ids). Attributes are Yes/No rows of the proposal table (English master questionnaire; translated display not documented). Vignette factors stored as trial_ fields. Respondent covariates (replication1.dta) cannot be linked (no id) and are not included.

Description: Dynata online samples in Brazil, Germany, South Africa and the US (Aug-Sep 2023, n=12,059) compared 3 pairs of proposals for a new global organization on internet content moderation, varying whether companies, scientists, civil-society organizations and individual internet users get a lot of say; they chose the most appropriate proposal and rated confidence in the organization (1-7).
Reference: Ecker-Ehrhardt, M., Verhaegen, S., & Quack, S. (2025). Nonstate actor inclusion and the social legitimacy of global governance institutions. International Studies Quarterly, 69(2), sqaf040.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/eckerehrhardt_2025.R. One of two experiments done by the same respondents (energy and internet tables share ids). Attributes are Yes/No rows of the proposal table (English master questionnaire; translated display not documented). Vignette factors stored as trial_ fields. Respondent covariates (replication1.dta) cannot be linked (no id) and are not included.

Description: 2,155 urban Ukrainian adults (Info Sapiens online panel, July 2020) rated 4 pairs of hypothetical local-election candidates described by name (gender and Ukrainian/Russian/neutral-sounding), priority issue, age, family status, children and political experience; yes/no vote intention and yes/no could-win for each candidate.
Reference: Erlich, A., & Beauvais, E. (2023). Explaining women's political underrepresentation in democracies with high levels of corruption. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(4), 804-822.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/erlich_2023.R (Study 2 only; Study 1 is a one-factor photo experiment). Speeders dropped as by the authors. Labels are the English translation in the .dta; survey ran in Ukrainian or Russian. Name gender/type recoverable from the name (header lists the type of each surname). Pair-2 'win' labels are Russian Da/Net in the file, mapped to 1/0.

Description: Democracy-promotion conjoint: 1,591 US adults on Prolific (2017 records) each saw up to 6 pairs of hypothetical autocratic countries varying oil, US alliance, trade ties, regime age, power concentration, leader type, elections, religion and military strength, and said yes/no to US military intervention, economic sanctions and democracy aid for each country.
Reference: Escribà-Folch, A., Muradova, L. H., & Rodon, T. (2021). The effects of autocratic characteristics on public opinion toward democracy promotion policies: A conjoint analysis. Foreign Policy Analysis, 17(1), 140-161.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/escribafolch_2021.R, built from the raw Qualtrics export. Three yes/no outcomes per profile (no choice column). The deposit has 1,591 records dated May-June 2017; the article reports 1,464 respondents in May-June 2016. Wave-2 task 5 dropped (levels not saved). attrpos_ from the recorded row order.

Description: Italian online panel respondents (wave 1, August-September 2020; 2,734 respondents, 1,237 in the authors' two-wave sample) chose which of two hypothetical individuals would be more likely to violate public-health guidelines (masks, distancing), over 4 pairs described by age, birthplace, economic status, party, sex, education and health (Italian text).
Reference: Ferwerda, J., Magni, G., Hooghe, L., & Marks, G. (2024). How crises shape circles of solidarity: Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy. Comparative Political Studies, 57(2), 356-381.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ferwerda_2023.R. Wave-1 task mapping: Q15.3 shows F-3 and Q15.5 shows F-2 (export question text; confirmed in the data by fit); the authors' read.qualtrics call pairs them in order, so their wave-1 estimates match two of four tasks to the wrong profiles. cov_panel_id links people to ferwerda_2023_vaccine_priority.

Description: Italian online panel respondents (wave 2, February 2021; 1,268 respondents, 1,236 in the authors' two-wave sample) chose which of two hypothetical Italian citizens should get priority for scarce COVID-19 vaccines, over 5 pairs described by age, birthplace, economic status, party, sex, education, health and occupation (Italian text).
Reference: Ferwerda, J., Magni, G., Hooghe, L., & Marks, G. (2024). How crises shape circles of solidarity: Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy. Comparative Political Studies, 57(2), 356-381.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ferwerda_2023.R. Export strips accents (Piu_ di 80, Poverta), restored. cov_panel_id links people to ferwerda_2023_guideline_violators.

Description: University of Milan students (2012 and 2013 waves, n=405) each chose which of two hypothetical candidates they would vote for in a fixed set of 27 pairs shown in random order; candidates varied in education, income, corruption record, and positions on taxes/social services and same-sex couples' rights (Italian text).
Reference: Franchino, F., & Zucchini, F. (2015). Voting in a multidimensional space: A conjoint analysis employing valence and ideology attributes of candidates. Political Science Research and Methods, 3(2), 221-241.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/franchino_2015.R. Attribute text is the Italian displayed text from the deposited instrument; codes verified against all 54 instrument profiles. Fixed fractional design of 27 pairs (trial_contest = pair number, task = display position). Two survey waves pooled (cov_survey_wave). Contact id and participation timestamp dropped.

Description: Taiwanese adults (wave 1, abstract condition, n=1,444) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical scenarios of Chinese aggression varying international military support (no/limited/full support from the US and Japan), sanctions, economic and military strength, readiness, morale and party unity, choosing one (perceived victory).
Reference: Fu, R. T., Lee, E. I., & Kao, K. Y. (2026). Do you think David can win against Goliath? Evidence on factors affecting popular perceptions of victory in Taiwan against Chinese aggression. Research & Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/fu_2026.R. Levels are the authors' English factor labels (displayed wording/language not in the deposit; article not retrieved). Question wording unknown. US and Japan support combined in one 6-level attribute. AMCEs reproduce the authors' run.log exactly.

Description: Taiwanese adults (wave 2, concrete condition, n=1,011) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical scenarios of Chinese aggression varying international military support (doing nothing/providing weapons/sending troops by the US and Japan), sanctions, economic and military strength, readiness, morale and party unity, choosing one (perceived victory).
Reference: Fu, R. T., Lee, E. I., & Kao, K. Y. (2026). Do you think David can win against Goliath? Evidence on factors affecting popular perceptions of victory in Taiwan against Chinese aggression. Research & Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/fu_2026.R. Levels are the authors' English factor labels (displayed wording/language not in the deposit; article not retrieved). Question wording unknown. US and Japan support combined in one 6-level attribute. AMCEs reproduce the authors' run.log exactly.

Description: Party executive-board members in Austria, Germany and Switzerland (n=1,856; 1,343 in the authors' 1,389-elite sample) made 8 forced choices between two fictitious aspirants for a prominent list place, varying age, gender, education, experience, issue and relative ideology, with a randomized share of women already on the list.
Reference: Gatto, M. A. C., & Radojevic, M. (2025). Choosing women: Party elites' preferences in the candidate selection process. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e36.
Notes: data/conjoint/gatto_2025.R. German level text as stored (French-language responses merged into German text; 6 profiles keep 'Diplôme universitaire'). Ideology wording is relative to the respondent and differs by cov_ideology_group ('moderater' kept, not recoded). trial_list_share = share of women already on the list, task-level. cov_in_authors_sample marks the article's 1,389 elites. Title/salutation, party, state dropped.

Description: Japanese respondents (March 2021, n=1,710) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical general-election scenarios varying remaining term, reason for dissolution, economic policy, pledge achievement, cabinet approval, surprise, economy and opposition coordination, choosing one.
Reference: Higashijima, M., Shimizu, N., Washida, H., & Yanai, Y. (2025). Partisan reactions to endogenous election timing: Evidence from conjoint experiments in Japan. Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/higashijima_2025.R. Japanese level text from the deposit's *_jpn columns (cabinet approval stored as % only). Outcome wording not deposited and article not retrieved: question unknown. Remaining term 0 occurs only with reason 'full term' (任期満了のため) and vice versa. Qualtrics ResponseIds and free text dropped; cov_party_group = the authors' government/independent/opposition grouping.

Description: Japanese respondents (January 2022, n=2,577) compared 8 pairs of hypothetical general-election scenarios varying remaining term, reason, economic policy, how the PM decided, cabinet approval, surprise, economy and opposition coordination, choosing one.
Reference: Higashijima, M., Shimizu, N., Washida, H., & Yanai, Y. (2025). Partisan reactions to endogenous election timing: Evidence from conjoint experiments in Japan. Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/higashijima_2025.R. Japanese level text from the deposit's *_jpn columns (cabinet approval stored as % only). Outcome wording not deposited and article not retrieved: question unknown. Remaining term 0 occurs only with how-decided 'term expired' (任期満了のため) and vice versa; reason 'full term' only with remaining term 0. The authors' code also forbids term 0 with other reasons, but 2,179 such profiles occur in the data (flagged). Qualtrics ResponseIds and free text dropped; cov_party_group = the authors' government/independent/opposition grouping.

Description: Market vendors in Malawi (face-to-face survey in 128 markets, n=2,527 with answers) compared 2 pairs of hypothetical civil society organizations varying where they were founded, the leader's former profession, funding source and party affiliation; they chose whose meetings they would attend and answered a second (scandal) question about the same pairs.
Reference: Hoellerbauer, S. (2023). Why join? How civil society organizations' attributes signal congruence and impact community engagement. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 10(1), 88-99.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hoellerbauer_2023.R. Level text from the deposit codebook (English); one leader level ('politician') is only named in the author's code. Verbatim outcome wording not deposited (article paywalled); choice_scandal is unfavourable (the author reverses it). Tasks with an unsaved attribute dropped; respondent ids re-keyed.

Description: Immigrant-admission conjoint: 1,621 US adults (Prolific, June 2023) each compared 4 pairs of described immigrants varying gender, sexuality, country wealth, skill, English, religion and reason for migrating; outcomes are which to admit, which shares US values, and 1-7 ratings of both.
Reference: Hoffmann, N. I., & Velasco, K. (2025). How sexuality affects evaluations of immigrant deservingness and cultural similarity: A conjoint survey experiment. Public Opinion Quarterly, 89(4), 1138-1153.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hoffmann_2025.R. Profiles were written descriptions; attr_ holds each embedded phrase as exported. Authors' sample filters applied; 1,621 respondents vs 1,650 in the article (29 dropped by the authors' code for expired Prolific age). Authors' Pew-raked weights not deposited.

Description: 2,209 US Prolific respondents (December 2020) each rated 10 pairs of hypothetical congressional candidates from their own party on a 7-point vote-likelihood scale; 8 attributes including a sexual-harassment scandal, under fully or partially randomized designs.
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., Markovich, Z., & Yamamoto, T. (2022). Does conjoint analysis mitigate social desirability bias? Political Analysis, 30(4), 535-549.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/horiuchi_2022.R (Study 2). trial_design random/constrained (constrained: only Scandal differs within a pair; in both arms exactly one candidate per pair has the scandal); trial_prime = face-to-face interview prime; trial_candidate_party. Attention-check failers kept (cov_attention_pass). Deposit contains IP addresses, GPS coordinates and Prolific IDs (dropped).

Description: 3,073 US MTurk respondents (December 2018) each rated 20 pairs of hypothetical athletic shoes described by 10 attributes including eco-friendly materials and gel cushioning, on a 7-point purchase-likelihood scale, under fully or partially randomized designs.
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., Markovich, Z., & Yamamoto, T. (2022). Does conjoint analysis mitigate social desirability bias? Political Analysis, 30(4), 535-549.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/horiuchi_2022.R (Study 1). trial_design: treat/control x random/constrained; in constrained arms only the focal attribute differs within a pair, and in all arms the focal attribute always differs. Attribute order recorded (attrpos_*). Wave-1 covariates merged on MTurk ID (then dropped); one duplicate worker dropped. Deposit contains MTurk IDs.

Description: 1,504 UK adults (Dynata online sample, May 2020) each chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical COVID-19 contact-tracing apps varying in data storage, storage duration, contacts and location uploaded, purpose and contact definition; half saw a data-breach prime first.
Reference: Horvath, L., Banducci, S., & James, O. (2022). Citizens' attitudes to contact tracing apps. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 9(1), 118-130.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/horvath_2022.R (Study 1 only; Study 2 is a one-question prime experiment). Decentralised apps carry fixed levels on four other attributes (observed restriction). trial_breach_prime = control/breach arm. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: 1,935 US heterosexual parents (online sample, August 2020) compared 4 pairs of vignettes describing a married couple with two children, varying childcare availability, each spouse's work status and earnings, division of chore time and the husband's share of traditionally feminine tasks; they chose the arrangement they would prefer and rated each couple's fairness (1-5).
Reference: Hutchinson, A., Khan, S., & Matfess, H. (2023). Childcare, work, and household labor during a pandemic: Evidence on parents' preferences in the United States. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 10(2), 155-173.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hutchinson_2023.R. Levels are the phrases inserted into the vignette; the vignette template and the exact choice wording are not in the deposit. 8 tasks with unsaved levels and 24 with no choice dropped. Respondent UUIDs re-keyed.

Description: US online panel respondents (Study 1, fielded 28-30 October 2023, after the Gaza ground invasion; 1,253 completes, 1,198 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical groups in a dispute they sympathized with more, over 11 pairs (the 11th repeats the first, flipped) described by 8 binary attributes such as majority religion, democracy and territorial goal.
Reference: Inouye, R., & Horiuchi, Y. (2026). Unraveling Americans' selective sympathies toward Israelis and Palestinians. International Studies Quarterly, 70(2), sqag027.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/inouye_2026.R (one script, two tables: Study 1 2023 and Study 2 2025, separate fieldings reported side by side). Profiles are mirror images by design (each attribute takes both levels within a task). cov_in_authors_sample from the authors' cleaned_data.rds ids; 23 exclusions per study are not explained by the deposited filter code.

Description: US online panel respondents (Study 2, fielded May 2025; 1,104 completes, 1,001 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical groups in a dispute they sympathized with more, over 11 pairs (the 11th repeats the first, flipped) described by 8 binary attributes such as majority religion, democracy and territorial goal. The same pairs were later judged for which group is more similar to Palestinian groups (pairs 1-5) or to the Israeli government (pairs 6-10).
Reference: Inouye, R., & Horiuchi, Y. (2026). Unraveling Americans' selective sympathies toward Israelis and Palestinians. International Studies Quarterly, 70(2), sqag027.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/inouye_2026.R (one script, two tables: Study 1 2023 and Study 2 2025, separate fieldings reported side by side). Profiles are mirror images by design (each attribute takes both levels within a task). cov_in_authors_sample from the authors' cleaned_data.rds ids; 23 exclusions per study are not explained by the deposited filter code.

Description: Russian migrants who left Russia in 2022 (convenience sample in 60+ countries, n=2,036) chose, in 2 tasks, which of two hypothetical Russian individuals (varying age, gender, children, profession, ethnic origin and motivation for emigrating) they preferred to help.
Reference: Kamalov, E., & Sergeeva, I. (2026). Helping emigrants flee a political crisis: How antiwar alignment shapes the aid preferences of wartime Russian migrants. Perspectives on Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kamalov_2026.R. Attribute text is the authors' English value labels; the survey was in Russian and the displayed text is not deposited. Outcome wording not deposited (article paraphrase). Deposit already restricted to the analysis sample.

Description: 1,203 US respondents from an MTurk convenience sample each judged up to 5 hypothetical (mayoral) elections between two candidates described by race, gender, age, political experience, career experience and, in randomly chosen partisan elections only, party; outcomes are a forced choice and a 0-100 competence rating of each candidate.
Reference: Kirkland, P. A., & Coppock, A. (2018). Candidate choice without party labels: New insights from conjoint survey experiments. Political Behavior, 40(3), 571-591.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kirkland_2018.R. Party label shown only in partisan elections (trial_election); blank attr_party = party not shown. Profile order inferred from row order. MTurk worker ID dropped and respondents re-keyed; one worker with two sets of contests and 4 contests left with one row by the authors' na.omit dropped. Derived dummies and policy/valence indices dropped. Companion table kirkland_2018_candidates_yougov.

Description: 1,200 US respondents from a YouGov nationally representative sample (survey weights included) each judged up to 5 hypothetical (mayoral) elections between two candidates described by race, gender, age, political experience, career experience and, in randomly chosen partisan elections only, party; outcomes are a forced choice and a 0-100 competence rating of each candidate.
Reference: Kirkland, P. A., & Coppock, A. (2018). Candidate choice without party labels: New insights from conjoint survey experiments. Political Behavior, 40(3), 571-591.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kirkland_2018.R. Party label shown only in partisan elections (trial_election); blank attr_party = party not shown. Profile order inferred from row order. Up to 5 contests per respondent (some fewer in the deposit). Derived dummies and policy/valence indices dropped. Companion table kirkland_2018_candidates_mturk.

Description: Candidates in the 2021 Danish municipal elections (n=2,141; 1,939 in the authors' completed-in-time sample) made 7 forced choices between two hypothetical council positions varying in position/influence, remuneration, workload and working environment (respect vs harassment vs sexism).
Reference: Kjøller, F. K., & Pedersen, L. H. (2025). The gendered cost of politics. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e59.
Notes: data/conjoint/kjoller_2025.R. Danish level text from the SPSS labels; position wording depends on municipality type (Copenhagen/magistrate/other), 8 texts for 3 levels. Partial respondents kept; cov_in_authors_sample marks the authors' analysis sample (gives 1,939 vs 1,938 reported). Deposit already omits name, email, municipality, party.

Description: Chinese online respondents (two waves, 2014-2015; n=2,846) compared 4 pairs of hypothetical foreign direct investment projects (home country, industry, entry mode, job impact, amount, local concessions, wage), choosing one and rating support for each on a 7-point scale.
Reference: Li, X., & Zeng, K. (2017). Individual preferences for FDI in developing countries: Experimental evidence from China. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 4(3), 195-205.
Notes: data/conjoint/li_2017.R. Chinese level text and per-task attribute order from Qualtrics embedded fields (GB18030 decoded), checked 1:1 against the authors' codes. Task and profile inferred from the file's 8 stacked blocks (blocks k and k+4 = task k; the only pairing with exactly one preferred project per task); which block was left is not recorded. 4 tasks without saved attribute text dropped. Qualtrics ResponseIds and occupation free text dropped.

Description: 31,112 adults in Egypt, Algeria, Morocco, Jordan, Tunisia and Libya (fall 2022) each rated one hypothetical candidate whose gender, background (civil society vs business), party goals (local development vs national economy) and success were randomized, on ten 0-10 scales (vote, endorsement, competence in several domains, others' vote).
Reference: Lust, E., & Benstead, L. J. (2024). Is the future female? Lessons from a conjoint experiment on voter preferences in six Arab countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lust_2024.R. One profile per respondent (2x2x2x2 factorial vignette). Level text is the Stata value labels (e.g. CSO, No Information); vignette prose, survey language and outcome wording were not deposited and the article could not be reached, so outcome questions are paraphrases of the authors' variable names. Saudi Arabia and Yemen pilots dropped as by the authors.

Description: Cint quota-sample adults in Australia, Canada, the UK and the US (March 2022; n=5,126 with usable answers in the conjoint arm) each rated four single scenarios of a manufacturing firm automating, which varied the product and its price change, high- and low-skilled job counts and wages; outcomes are perceived fairness and whether they would decide the same as CEO (both 1-5).
Reference: Magistro, B., Loewen, P., Bonikowski, B., Borwein, S., & Lee-Whiting, B. (2024). Attitudes toward automation and the demand for policies addressing job loss: The effects of information about trade-offs. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(4), 783-798.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/magistro_2024.R. Single-profile rating design (profile = 1). Four countries pooled as in the authors' analysis; wage levels carry country currency, price is the stored bare number (display format with currency not recoverable), product names in French for French-Canadian respondents. Price levels are conditional on the product. 20 respondents with unsaved attribute values dropped; Qualtrics ResponseId dropped.

Description: Candidate conjoint: 3,096 Italian adults in wave 2 (May-June 2019) of the Siena/GfK Italy probability panel each compared 2 pairs of hypothetical European Parliament candidates varying 8 traits (gender, job, communication style, social skills, integrity, competence, view of role, leadership) and chose which they would prefer to win a seat.
Reference: Martini, S., & Olmastroni, F. (2021). From the lab to the poll: The use of survey experiments in political research. Italian Political Science Review / Rivista Italiana di Scienza Politica, 51(2), 231-249.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/martini_2021.R. Built from the deposit's full-sample '_artisan' file (3,096 respondents); the article's main models use 2,676, dropping the 420 respondents who saw a rare 'artisan' job level (undocumented). Labels are the authors' English translations (respondents saw Italian). The 7-point rating is deposited only as an undocumented 0/1 split, so it is not built. Task inferred from candidate number 1-4.

Description: Online panel respondents in Kenya and Malawi (Qualtrics, March-April 2022; 390 respondents) compared images of polling-station vote tally sheets in 3 pairs, varying signatures of the presiding officer, ruling- and opposition-party agents and an observer, and crossed-out corrections on either party's tally. Outcomes: which sheet is more reliable, plus 1-5 ratings of misconduct likelihood and four reasons.
Reference: Mbozi, F. (2024). When do voters see fraud? Evaluating the effects of poll supervision on perceptions of integrity. Journal of Experimental Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mbozi_2024.R. Image conjoint: profiles were generated tally-sheet pictures; attr_ levels are the author's coding of the manipulated features (decoded from image file names), worded after the article. Vote numbers on the images (large/small difference) are not stored. Kenya and Malawi pooled (cov_country) as in the article; party roles stand for DPP/Jubilee (ruling) and MCP/ODM (opposition).

Description: German voters of the five 2005-2013 Bundestag parties (Bilendi online panel, December 2023-January 2024; 4,028 respondents) rated three hypothetical members of parliament, one at a time, varying gender, marital status, party, terms served, mandate type and disclosed outside activity and income. Outcomes: four 1-7 agreement ratings (represents voters' interests, competent, represents own or third-party interests, hardworking).
Reference: Neisser, C., & Wehrhöfer, N. (2026). Outside income as a signal: Evidence from politicians and voters. The Review of Economics and Statistics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neisser_2026.R. Single-profile rating design (profile = 1). German level text from Stata value labels; mandate level stores only the lead ('Über ein Direktmandat') because the gendered continuation is truncated in the label. Outcome wording is a paraphrase from truncated variable labels. Ratings kept raw 1-7 (authors standardize). cov_survey_weight recomputed from the authors' do-file.

Description: US MTurk workers (April 2020, n=984) compared 15 pairs of hypothetical job offers varying the state governor's COVID-19 response, location, company size, state partisanship, salary and company culture; they chose the more attractive offer and rated each offer's attractiveness (1-5).
Reference: Nelson, M. J., & Witko, C. (2020). Government reputational effects of COVID-19 public health actions: A job opportunity evaluation conjoint experiment. Journal of Behavioral Public Administration, 3(1).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nelson_2020.R. Level text from the article (Figure 1 example trial, note 6); two location levels from article prose and the two Trump political-climate levels written by analogy with the displayed Clinton ones. Rating uses the authors' recode of non-ordered Qualtrics codes. Qualtrics ResponseId dropped, ids re-keyed.

Description: 1,037 US Democrats and Republicans each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical candidates showing party plus 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 further attributes (gender, profession, age, family, race, military service, education, abortion and spending stances), testing how partisan voting changes with profile information.
Reference: Peterson, E. (2017). The role of the information environment in partisan voting. Journal of Politics, 79(4), 1191-1204.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/peterson_2017.R. attr_party rebuilt from the authors' copartisan flag and respondent party (display wording assumed Democrat/Republican). Blank attr_ = not shown in that task (trial_information_condition = number shown). No questionnaire; sample provider/date and choice wording undocumented. 69 tasks with no choice dropped.

Description: U.S. adults (Lucid, n=984) and U.S. State Department employees (n=147), Feb-Jun 2023, compared 6 pairs of hypothetical countries (reason, regime, religion, U.S. ally, military capability, trade), choosing against which military action is more justified and rating each 0-10.
Reference: Scholten, M., & Zhirkov, K. (2026). Public and expert preferences in survey experiments in foreign policy: Evidence from parallel conjoint analyses. Political Science Research and Methods, 14, 1011-1018.
Notes: data/conjoint/scholten_2025_foreign_policy.R. Mass and expert samples in one table (cov_sample), as the authors pool them. Task inferred from row order. 132 tasks with no recorded choice are blank (the authors count them as 0). Attribute order randomized but not deposited. Mass-sample AMCEs reproduce the authors' log.

Description: 6,047 online-panel respondents in the US, Germany, Italy, Poland and Brazil (August 2020) each chose which of two hypothetical COVID-19 patients to prioritize for intensive care in up to 4 pairs; patients varied in age, gender, children, job, arrival time, survival chance and partisanship (left party, right party or none).
Reference: Stoetzer, L. F., Munzert, S., Lowe, W., Cali, B., Gohdes, A. R., Helbling, M., Maxwell, R., & Traunmueller, R. (2023). Affective partisan polarization and moral dilemmas during the COVID-19 pandemic. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(2), 429-436.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/stoetzer_2023.R. Five countries pooled with cov_country; partisanship names a country-specific left/right party. Level text is the deposit's English labels (screens were in EN/DE/IT/PL/PT-BR); question wording not deposited. Patient B's arrival follows patient A's. Country-size weight dropped. 368 of 6,415 respondents answered no pair.

Description: 1,203 US Prolific respondents (February 2023) each assessed 8 pairs of countries in hypothetical territorial disputes, described by threat type (public, private, none), mobilization, domestic hawkishness, leader popularity, military capability, stakes, regime type, US relations, leader traits and past dispute behaviour; outcomes are a 0-100 estimate that each country stands firm and a choice of which is more likely to stand firm.
Reference: Takei, M. (2024). Audience costs and the credibility of public versus private threats in international crises. International Studies Quarterly, 68(3), sqae091.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/takei_2024.R. Level text = sentence fragments from appendix Tables 3-4 (stems omitted). Wide popular* columns contradict the long `unpopular` label; the long label (used in the authors' models) is followed. Unrealistic combinations (US as dictatorship) allowed by design. Weights not deposited.

Description: TRI-POL panel respondents in Argentina (online panel, wave 3; 977 respondents, 975 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical families they would prefer as next-door neighbours in 12 pairs described by 10 attributes: regional identity, ideology, birthplace, couple type, party support, education, recycling, pet ownership, religion and politicisation.
Reference: Torcal, M., Comellas, J. M., & Vrânceanu, A. (2026). Social distance as a product of political identities: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026.R (one script, five country tables; attribute sets differ by country). Level text = the panel file's English value labels, shorter than the displayed phrasing (e.g. 'Left' shown as 'Left-wing', 'PSOE' as 'PSOE supporter'); respondents saw the es translation. Paper forthcoming in PSRM, no DOI yet. Wording/design from the TRI-POL wave-3 questionnaire on OSF (osf.io/3t7jz).

Description: TRI-POL panel respondents in Chile (online panel, wave 3; 921 respondents, 916 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical families they would prefer as next-door neighbours in 12 pairs described by 10 attributes: regional identity, ideology, birthplace, couple type, party support, education, recycling, pet ownership, religion and politicisation.
Reference: Torcal, M., Comellas, J. M., & Vrânceanu, A. (2026). Social distance as a product of political identities: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026.R (one script, five country tables; attribute sets differ by country). Level text = the panel file's English value labels, shorter than the displayed phrasing (e.g. 'Left' shown as 'Left-wing', 'PSOE' as 'PSOE supporter'); respondents saw the es translation. Paper forthcoming in PSRM, no DOI yet. Wording/design from the TRI-POL wave-3 questionnaire on OSF (osf.io/3t7jz).

Description: TRI-POL panel respondents in Italy (online panel, wave 3; 997 respondents, 986 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical families they would prefer as next-door neighbours in 12 pairs described by 11 (incl. vaccination) attributes: regional identity, ideology, birthplace, couple type, party support, education, recycling, pet ownership, religion and politicisation.
Reference: Torcal, M., Comellas, J. M., & Vrânceanu, A. (2026). Social distance as a product of political identities: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026.R (one script, five country tables; attribute sets differ by country). Level text = the panel file's English value labels, shorter than the displayed phrasing (e.g. 'Left' shown as 'Left-wing', 'PSOE' as 'PSOE supporter'); respondents saw the it translation. Paper forthcoming in PSRM, no DOI yet. Wording/design from the TRI-POL wave-3 questionnaire on OSF (osf.io/3t7jz).

Description: TRI-POL panel respondents in Portugal (online panel, wave 3; 823 respondents, 821 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical families they would prefer as next-door neighbours in 12 pairs described by 10 attributes: regional identity, ideology, birthplace, couple type, party support, education, recycling, pet ownership, religion and politicisation.
Reference: Torcal, M., Comellas, J. M., & Vrânceanu, A. (2026). Social distance as a product of political identities: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026.R (one script, five country tables; attribute sets differ by country). Level text = the panel file's English value labels, shorter than the displayed phrasing (e.g. 'Left' shown as 'Left-wing', 'PSOE' as 'PSOE supporter'); respondents saw the pt translation. Paper forthcoming in PSRM, no DOI yet. Wording/design from the TRI-POL wave-3 questionnaire on OSF (osf.io/3t7jz).

Description: TRI-POL panel respondents in Spain (online panel, wave 3; 1,080 respondents, 1,071 in the authors' sample) chose which of two hypothetical families they would prefer as next-door neighbours in 12 pairs described by 11 (incl. language) attributes: regional identity, ideology, birthplace, couple type, party support, education, recycling, pet ownership, religion and politicisation.
Reference: Torcal, M., Comellas, J. M., & Vrânceanu, A. (2026). Social distance as a product of political identities: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026.R (one script, five country tables; attribute sets differ by country). Level text = the panel file's English value labels, shorter than the displayed phrasing (e.g. 'Left' shown as 'Left-wing', 'PSOE' as 'PSOE supporter'); respondents saw the es translation. Paper forthcoming in PSRM, no DOI yet. Wording/design from the TRI-POL wave-3 questionnaire on OSF (osf.io/3t7jz).

Description: Residents of Paipote (Atacama, Chile) surveyed after the 2015 floods (210 respondents, 204 with answers) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 8 pairs described by ideology, profession, gender, age, political experience and whether they would hand out economic aid (Spanish text); flood exposure is the natural-experiment treatment.
Reference: Visconti, G. (2022). After the flood: Disasters, ideological voting and electoral choices in Chile. Political Behavior, 44(4), 1985-2004.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/visconti_2022.R. Question wording not in the deposit (article paywalled); choice = the source's 'selected'. 161 pairs have neither candidate selected (kept; whether 'neither' was an offered option is unknown; the same author's 2017 Santiago study, visconti_2021, recorded a volunteered 'neither'). The author's ideology x flood-exposure AMCEs reproduce exactly.

Description: Vehicle-emission policy-package conjoint: 2,034 Swiss residents (IPSOS online quota sample, December 2017) each compared 5 pairs of packages varying energy label, registration ban, road pricing, car tax, earmarking, information campaign, implementation year, test phase and expert involvement; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-7 agreement rating, under an EV-promotion or emission-reduction frame.
Reference: Wicki, M., Huber, R. A., & Bernauer, T. (2020). Can policy-packaging increase public support for costly policies? Insights from a choice experiment on policies against vehicle emissions. Journal of Public Policy, 40(4), 599-625.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wicki_2020.R. Respondents saw German, French or Italian; attr_ text is the English characteristic text of the article's Table 1 mapped from the deposit's codes. Level shares are unequal and correlated (restrictions observed). Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. A corrigendum (JPP 40(4), 626-627) was not checked.

Description: Supreme Court nominee conjoint: 9,359 US adults (Lucid, December 2022) each chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical nominees varying age, gender, position, partisanship, race/ethnicity, religion, law school and clerkship, with the Court's assumed partisan composition (none, 4-4, 6-2 Republican, 6-2 Democratic) randomized between respondents.
Reference: Wu, V. Y., & Horiuchi, Y. (2026). The Supreme Court's partisan composition affects how Americans evaluate nominees: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Journal of Law and Courts, 1-24.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wu_2026.R, built from the raw Qualtrics export with the authors' filters. The paper's n = 9,895 counts respondents passing screening; 536 of them did not finish and the authors' conjoint data (and this table) keep the 9,359 completers. Partisanship and race levels were drawn with unequal weights. attrpos_ recovered from level text.

Description: US Republican and Independent registered voters (Toluna/Qualtrics daily samples, January 2021; n=1,883, 1,481 good completes) chose between two hypothetical Republican congressional primary candidates varying profession, military service, religion, race/ethnicity, gender, age and whether the candidate says Trump won or lost the 2020 election; 3 pairs each.
Reference: Arceneaux, K., & Truex, R. (2023). Donald Trump and the lie. Perspectives on Politics, 21(3), 863-879.
Notes: data/conjoint/arceneaux_2023.R. Only Republicans and Independents saw the conjoint. Authors' sample = cov_good_complete 1 (1,481); 402 others kept (6 speeders, 396 without completion code). Authors' entropy-balancing weights are computed in their script, not deposited. Level shares uneven (religion, age). Panel IDs and free-text answers dropped.

Description: US adults (SSI, Nov-Dec 2016, n=2,786) compared two hypothetical US Senate candidates on 4 core attributes (age, party, health care, same-sex marriage) plus a randomly assigned number (0-35) of irrelevant filler attributes; 15 pairs each, forced choice plus a 1-7 vote rating.
Reference: Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., Hopkins, D. J., & Yamamoto, T. (2019). Beyond the breaking point? Survey satisficing in conjoint experiments. Political Science Research and Methods, 9(1), 53-71.
Notes: data/conjoint/bansak_2019.R. Filler attributes not drawn for a respondent are '(not shown)'; trial_n_fillers = number of fillers shown (fixed per respondent). Attribute order randomized, not recorded. The Study 1 MTurk sample is held (numeric codes without labels). Validator PII hint on attr_email_time_of_day is a false alarm (time of day).

Description: US MTurk workers (March 2017, n=3,307) compared two hypothetical hotel rooms on 4 core attributes (floor, view, furniture, internet) plus a randomly assigned number (0-18) of meaningful filler attributes; 15 pairs each, forced choice plus a 1-7 rating.
Reference: Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., Hopkins, D. J., & Yamamoto, T. (2019). Beyond the breaking point? Survey satisficing in conjoint experiments. Political Science Research and Methods, 9(1), 53-71.
Notes: data/conjoint/bansak_2019.R. Filler attributes not drawn for a respondent are '(not shown)'; trial_n_fillers = number of fillers shown (fixed per respondent). Attribute order randomized, not recorded. The Study 1 MTurk sample is held (numeric codes without labels). Core AMCEs at 0 fillers reproduce the article (ocean view 0.175, paid internet -0.303).

Description: Duke lab participants (eye-tracking, Jun-Sep 2022, n=145) chose between two hypothetical US political candidates (age, gender, party, prior political experience, job, education, positions on taxes on the wealthy and gun control); 60 pairs each in four within-subject conditions that add incongruent or nonsensical profiles.
Reference: Bansak, K., & Jenke, L. (2025). Odd profiles in conjoint experimental designs: Effects on survey-taking attention and behavior. Political Analysis, 33(4), 315-338.
Notes: data/conjoint/bansak_2025.R. One table per scenario; the same participants did both. trial_condition = Normal/Incongruent/Nonsensical/Combined (blocks of 15), trial_block = block order. Article reports 147 participants; 145 in this scenario file. Eye-tracking measures not included. Attribute order randomized, not recorded.

Description: Duke lab participants (eye-tracking, Jun-Sep 2022, n=142) chose between two hypothetical immigrants applying for US residency (age, gender, language, migration type, origin, job, education, reason for settling); 60 pairs each in four within-subject conditions that add incongruent or nonsensical profiles.
Reference: Bansak, K., & Jenke, L. (2025). Odd profiles in conjoint experimental designs: Effects on survey-taking attention and behavior. Political Analysis, 33(4), 315-338.
Notes: data/conjoint/bansak_2025.R. One table per scenario; the same participants did both. trial_condition = Normal/Incongruent/Nonsensical/Combined (blocks of 15), trial_block = block order. Article reports 147 participants; 142 in this scenario file. Eye-tracking measures not included. Attribute order randomized, not recorded.

Description: Face-to-face respondents in three northern Afghan provinces (2016-2017; n=2,485) compared 3 pairs of hypothetical political leaders varying gender, education, age, ethnicity, professional experience and birthplace, choosing one and rating each 1-5 for suitability, after a randomly assigned prime (control, bribery, nepotism or insecurity).
Reference: Bhatia, J., & Monroe, S. L. (2025). Candidate qualifications and out-group support: Evidence from Afghanistan. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bhatia_2025.R. Built from Afghan_Data_All.csv (all four prime arms, trial_prime); choice and rating totals match the authors' conjoint_clean.csv. Level text English as deposited (ethnicity level 'Pashto' as stored); the survey ran in Dari or Pashto. Some levels clearly under-sampled (Military, Kandahar, age 28). Village, district and birth-town text dropped (PII). Article not read; DOI from poliscidata listing.

Description: Spanish adults in an online quota sample (June 2016, n=2,248) evaluated 3 pairs of hypothetical mayoral candidates varying sex, party, qualities, economic performance and corruption. Outcomes: 0-10 probability of voting for each candidate, and a forced choice between them.
Reference: Breitenstein, S. (2019). Choosing the crook: A conjoint experiment on voting for corrupt politicians. Research & Politics, 6(1).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/breitenstein_2019.R. Level text in Spanish as displayed. Speeder tasks kept; trial_page_seconds lets users apply the authors' rule (reproduces the article's 12,284 profiles). Survey ids re-keyed.

Description: British YouGov respondents (February 2015; n=1,719) each made 5 forced choices between two hypothetical MPs varying in local roots, party and ideological position, time spent on constituency work, main policy influence, policy interests and gender (pronoun).
Reference: Campbell, R., Cowley, P., Vivyan, N., & Wagner, M. (2019). Why friends and neighbors? Explaining the electoral appeal of local roots. The Journal of Politics, 81(3), 937-951.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/campbell_2019.R (Study 2 only; Study 1 is a between-subjects vignette, not built). Level text is the deposited display text (HTML fragments, bold tags removed); attr_time is rebuilt from the screenshot template and the deposited day counts. Gender is carried only by the pronoun (He/She). Parliamentary constituency, browser/device and YouGov refno dropped.

Description: US adults (Lucid quota sample, July-August 2019; 1,485 answering of 1,505 assigned) chose which of two fictitious candidates they would rather vote for over 5 pairs, varying two political priorities (12 possible, populist and non-populist) and positions on legal immigration, military intervention, taxing the rich and free trade.
Reference: Castanho Silva, B., Neuner, F. G., & Wratil, C. (2023). Populism and candidate support in the US: The effects of "thin" and "host" ideology. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 10(3), 438-447.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/castanhosilva_2023.R. Each candidate showed a first and second priority; the deposit keeps only which 2 of 12 were shown (not their order), stored as 12 attr_priority_* columns holding the priority text or "(not shown)". Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed. Attention-check answer kept (cov_attention_check; 3 = pass).

Description: German YouGov respondents (October-November 2021; n=1,558) made 4 forced choices between two government climate proposals varying the policy, timing of costs, tax design, complexity, GDP cost or benefit, who proposed it and public support.
Reference: Devine, D., Stoker, G., & Jennings, W. (2024). Political trust and climate policy choice: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Journal of Public Policy, 44(2), 327-343.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/devine_2024.R. Respondents saw German; attr_ text is English: full master-instrument value labels for policy, timing, complexity and public support, but the article's Table 1 short labels for pricing, GDP and recommended-by (the .dta labels are cut at 80 characters). attrpos_ from C2b_attr_order (policy always first; reading as display order inferred). Covariates are value-label text.

Description: US adults on Prolific (October 2024; 4,013 with any answered task, 3,916 in the authors' sample) chose which of two laid-off workers (age, gender, education, parental class) should get more government income assistance and rated support for each on 0-10; 5 pairs plus a repeat of pair 1, half saw an ICT/labour-market information screen first.
Reference: Diessner, S., Durazzi, N., Filetti, F. D., Hope, D., Kleider, H., Limberg, J., & Tonelli, S. (2026). Welfare state deservingness in the era of mass higher education. Public Opinion Quarterly.
Notes: data/conjoint/diessner_2026.R. Task 6 is task 1 repeated with worker order reversed; its profiles are rebuilt from task 1 (trial_repeat = 1). Unfinished and speeding respondents kept with cov_finished and cov_duration_sec (authors: finished and > 180 s = 3,916, reproduced). trial_ict_info = information-screen arm. Qualtrics ResponseId and free-text feedback dropped.

Description: 853 US county party chairs (Democratic and Republican) judged 10 pairs of hypothetical state-legislative primary candidates, each shown by name plus four randomly drawn attributes (background, issue positions, or a descriptor). Outcome: which candidate would fare best in their party's primary in their area.
Reference: Doherty, D., Dowling, C. M., & Miller, M. G. (2019). Do local party chairs think women and minority candidates can win? Evidence from a conjoint experiment. The Journal of Politics, 81(4), 1282-1297.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/doherty_2019.R. Names signal gender and race/ethnicity (authors' coding). Attributes not drawn for a profile = '(not shown)'. Occupation, political experience, military service and the friends-describe-as descriptor are stored only as the authors' classes (displayed wording not in the anonymized file). Noised county context variables and the 0-100 follow-up dropped.

Description: British YouGov respondents (June 2014; n=1,962) each saw 5 hypothetical marginal-constituency contests between the current MP and the main challenger (party, age, gender, former job; MP's good or bad conduct) and said whom they would vote for, with third-party and abstention options.
Reference: Eggers, A. C., Vivyan, N., & Wagner, M. (2018). Corruption, accountability, and gender: Do female politicians face higher standards in public life? The Journal of Politics, 80(1), 321-326.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/eggers_2018.R. Profile 1 = current MP, profile 2 = challenger; attr_conduct shown for the MP only ("(not shown)" for the challenger). Party pairs restricted (MP Labour or Conservative, challenger a different party). Challenger ages in the data (38/51/62) differ from the article text (40/52/64); the data match the article's screenshot. Wording from the accepted manuscript (not deposited).

Description: Japanese adults (online survey; n=2,576) chose which of two hypothetical House of Representatives candidates they would vote for and which would benefit them, their prefecture and Japan, 8 pairs each; candidates varied by university, high school, career, years in job, incumbency, father's job, policy, surname and gender, many defined relative to the respondent's own prefecture.
Reference: Gagnon, E., Ikeda, F., & McElwain, K. M. (2025). Preferring national elites or local candidates: A conjoint analysis of voter heuristics. Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/gagnon_2025.R (survey 1). Japanese level text as stored; six attributes were piped from Qualtrics embedded fields not in the export, so their text keeps a placeholder such as [respondent_prefecture]の高校 (= a high school in the respondent's own prefecture); the concrete prefecture/university names are not deposited. Article not reachable; N not checked. 44 unfinished respondents kept (cov_finished).

Description: Japanese adults (Rakuten Insight panel follow-up survey; n=2,578) chose between two hypothetical male candidates (surname, local/non-local/elite biography, party, years in job), 3 pairs each, for vote choice and for which would act more on six policy issues and on their prefecture's issues.
Reference: Gagnon, E., Ikeda, F., & McElwain, K. M. (2025). Preferring national elites or local candidates: A conjoint analysis of voter heuristics. Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/gagnon_2025.R (survey 2). Biography text filled with each respondent's own embedded values (their prefecture, Tokyo/Osaka, local national university, UTokyo/KyotoU), so it is the text shown. First name kept as attr_first_name; all profiles male. Raw export contains IP addresses, GPS coordinates, panel tokens, postcodes and free text: all dropped. Article not reachable; N not checked.

Description: 14,324 respondents from YouGov and partner panels in 20 countries (2022-2024) each chose between 7 pairs of hypothetical candidates varying gender, age, political experience, children, ideology, occupation and country of origin, for national or local office.
Reference: Gothreau, C., & Laustsen, L. (2026). Women and left-wing citizens prefer women candidates: Testing consistency and psychological processes across twenty diverse countries. Public Opinion Quarterly, 90(SI), 989-1016.
Notes: data/conjoint/gothreau_2026.R. 20 countries pooled (cov_country) as in the article; English labels stored, respondents saw national languages. trial_wave separates the main fielding, US wave 2 and 2024 follow-ups (the latter two with randomized attribute order, trial_attr_order unmapped). Some levels had double weight. Free-text comments dropped.

Description: Adults in Kazakhstan (interviewer-administered, Jan-Feb 2021, n=3,000) compared two hypothetical immigrants on 10 attributes (education, gender, ethnicity, language, reason, profession, experience, religion, intended stay, legal status); 3 pairs each, forced choice plus two 1-7 ratings of each immigrant.
Reference: Higashijima, M., Igarashi, A., & Woo, Y. (2026). Do Muslim citizens welcome fundamentalist Muslim immigrants? Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Kazakhstan. Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/higashijima_2026.R. Attribute text = authors' English labels (Russian/Kazakh display text not deposited). Rating wordings not deposited; rating_sim meaning undocumented. Education-profession and ethnicity-language restrictions. All respondents kept; article analyses Muslims (2,097). Article not read (login wall). Empty name/phone columns in deposit.

Description: English adults (Deltapoll, February 2021; 4,012 respondents) chose between and rated 5 pairs of hypothetical parliamentary candidates, each involved in a controversy (authoritarian rhetoric or another misdemeanour), varying how and by whom other MPs reacted, gender, party and ministerial experience.
Reference: Hobolt, S. B., & Osnabrügge, M. (2024). Countering authoritarian behavior in democracies. Political Behavior, 47(2), 781-800.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hobolt_2024.R. Level text from the article's Table 1 (the .dta value labels are shortened versions). rating restored to 1-7 from the authors' 0-1 rescaling; wording and anchors unknown. cov_threat_* are the eight 1-10 threat-to-democracy items (97 = don't know), reproducing the article's Table 2 means.

Description: Japanese adults (Research Now online panel, December 2014, before the House of Representatives election; 1,951 respondents) chose which of two hypothetical parties they would support over 5 pairs of manifestos built from the real parties' positions on 9 policy issues (consumption tax, employment, monetary/fiscal policy, growth strategy, nuclear restart, TPP, collective self-defense, constitutional revision, seat reduction).
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., Smith, D. M., & Yamamoto, T. (2018). Measuring voters' multidimensional policy preferences with conjoint analysis: Application to Japan's 2014 election. Political Analysis, 26(2), 190-209.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/horiuchi_2018.R. Level text is the Japanese shown to respondents (Qualtrics F- fields); English translations with the parties holding each position are in the authors' HSY-preprocess.R (inside the deposit archive). Attribute order randomized and recorded (attrpos_). Sample filter follows the authors' HSY-makedata.R; their entropy-balancing weights are not stored. Codebook (codebook.pdf) is inside ReplicationArchive.tar.gz.

Description: UK creative-sector professional respondents (Dynata; n=268) imagined selling rights in a landscape photo to a guidebook publisher and made 6 forced choices between two contracts varying price (25/50 GBP) and four yes/no rights transfers (attribution, issuing copies, reproduction, derivative works).
Reference: Kantorowicz, J., Kantorowicz-Reznichenko, E., & Nahmias, Y. (2025). The price of creativity: A conjoint experiment in copyrights. Journal of Public Policy, 45(2), 245-269.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kantorowicz_2025.R (one script, three sample tables, analysed separately by the authors; price currency differs). Task and profile inferred from the cjoint-style row order (verified pairs; task order assumed). Question wording paraphrased (supplement not obtained). Attribute order randomized per respondent but not deposited. Education codes unlabelled (dropped).

Description: UK general-population respondents (Dynata; n=718) imagined selling rights in a landscape photo to a guidebook publisher and made 6 forced choices between two contracts varying price (25/50 GBP) and four yes/no rights transfers (attribution, issuing copies, reproduction, derivative works).
Reference: Kantorowicz, J., Kantorowicz-Reznichenko, E., & Nahmias, Y. (2025). The price of creativity: A conjoint experiment in copyrights. Journal of Public Policy, 45(2), 245-269.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kantorowicz_2025.R (one script, three sample tables, analysed separately by the authors; price currency differs). Task and profile inferred from the cjoint-style row order (verified pairs; task order assumed). Question wording paraphrased (supplement not obtained). Attribute order randomized per respondent but not deposited. Education codes unlabelled (dropped).

Description: US creative-sector professional respondents (Dynata; n=278) imagined selling rights in a landscape photo to a guidebook publisher and made 6 forced choices between two contracts varying price (25/50 USD) and four yes/no rights transfers (attribution, issuing copies, reproduction, derivative works).
Reference: Kantorowicz, J., Kantorowicz-Reznichenko, E., & Nahmias, Y. (2025). The price of creativity: A conjoint experiment in copyrights. Journal of Public Policy, 45(2), 245-269.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kantorowicz_2025.R (one script, three sample tables, analysed separately by the authors; price currency differs). Task and profile inferred from the cjoint-style row order (verified pairs; task order assumed). Question wording paraphrased (supplement not obtained). Attribute order randomized per respondent but not deposited. Education codes unlabelled (dropped).

Description: Hong Kong respondents (wave 1, before the June 2020 National Security Law; n=1,522) chose between two packages of government responses to the 2019 protest demands bundled with economic relief measures (9 attributes); 5 pairs each, forced choice.
Reference: Kobayashi, T., Song, J., & Chan, P. (2021). Does repression undermine opposition demands? The case of the Hong Kong National Security Law. Japanese Journal of Political Science, 22(4), 268-286.
Notes: data/conjoint/kobayashi_2021.R. One table per wave (attribute sets differ, separate samples); the 9 shared attributes allow stacking. Attribute text = authors' English labels from their replication R code; displayed language, question wording, firm and dates not deposited; article paywalled, not read.

Description: Hong Kong respondents (wave 2, after the June 2020 National Security Law; n=1,541) chose between two packages of government responses to the 2019 protest demands bundled with economic relief measures (13 attributes; plus NSL enforcement: target, imprisonment term, jury trial, authority in charge); 5 pairs each, forced choice.
Reference: Kobayashi, T., Song, J., & Chan, P. (2021). Does repression undermine opposition demands? The case of the Hong Kong National Security Law. Japanese Journal of Political Science, 22(4), 268-286.
Notes: data/conjoint/kobayashi_2021.R. One table per wave (attribute sets differ, separate samples); the 9 shared attributes allow stacking. Attribute text = authors' English labels from their replication R code; displayed language, question wording, firm and dates not deposited; article paywalled, not read.

Description: German adults from a Bilendi online panel (December 2022, n=4,374) compared 4 pairs of plans for border measures at Germany's borders, varying measure, neighbouring country and justification. Outcomes: choice of the plan they would more likely support, and a 0-10 rating of each plan.
Reference: Lipps, J., Sczepanski, R., & Malet, G. (2025). Understanding preferences over borders. International Studies Quarterly, 69(1), sqaf003.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lipps_2025.R. Screen position not deposited: profile numbers are arbitrary labels (not usable for position effects). Level text = the article's English descriptions mapped from the deposit's short codes; respondents saw German. Respondent-location distance variables dropped as identifying.

Description: Chinese government officials (n=299 with answers) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical candidates for an entry-level government post, varying gender, party membership, college, degree, award, work experience and father's occupation. Outcomes: which candidate to select, plus 1-5 ratings of suitability, leadership and task implementation.
Reference: Liu, H. (2019). The logic of authoritarian political selection: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in China. Political Science Research and Methods, 7(4), 853-870.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/liu_2019.R. Level text = English Stata value labels (display language not documented). Question wording and rating anchors not deposited (article paywalled). 33 of 332 respondents answered nothing and are omitted.

Description: 1,263 German Kieskompas panel respondents (April 2023) chose between 5 pairs of school-curriculum reform proposals from civic groups in a hypothetical consultation; profiles varied an AI-generated face (gender, age, ethnicity), LGBT+/trans marker, group name, proposal, justification, national support and a foreign country.
Reference: López Ortega, A., & Turnbull-Dugarte, S. J. (2025). Selectively (il)liberal: Theory and evidence on nativist disidentification. Political Science Research and Methods, 14(3), 789-815.
Notes: data/conjoint/lopezortega_2025.R. One table per country (Dutch vs German level text); the authors pool NL and DE. Face stored as image file id with the authors' gender/age/ethnicity coding; LGBT marker is the authors' code. Choice wording not deposited. Deposit has 1,263 respondents vs 1,358 in the article. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: 1,140 Dutch Kieskompas panel respondents (August 2022) chose between 5 pairs of school-curriculum reform proposals from civic groups in a hypothetical consultation; profiles varied an AI-generated face (gender, age, ethnicity), LGBT+/trans marker, group name, proposal, justification, national support and a foreign country.
Reference: López Ortega, A., & Turnbull-Dugarte, S. J. (2025). Selectively (il)liberal: Theory and evidence on nativist disidentification. Political Science Research and Methods, 14(3), 789-815.
