Notes: data/conjoint/lopezortega_2025.R. One table per country (Dutch vs German level text); the authors pool NL and DE. Face stored as image file id with the authors' gender/age/ethnicity coding; LGBT marker is the authors' code. Choice wording not deposited. Deposit has 1,140 respondents vs 1,169 in the article. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: US adults (Lucid, December 2022, n=2,076) chose among three hypothetical US vacation destinations (temperature, attractions, travel time, 2020 state election result, recent state news incl. democratic backsliding laws, community type) and rated interest in each; 10 tasks, with a 'none' option.
Reference: Miller, D. R., & Smith, S. D. (2024). (Small D-democratic) vacation, all I ever wanted? The effect of democratic backsliding on leisure travel in the American states. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12, 99-109.
Notes: data/conjoint/miller_2024.R. Study 1 only (Study 2 is not a conjoint). Built from the raw Qualtrics export (attribute order recorded as attrpos_), cross-checked against the authors' cleaned file. Opt-out 'None of these destinations'. The authors stripped an apostrophe from two 'voters ability' levels. Backsliding vs baseline difference (-3.3 points) reproduces the article.

Description: US MTurk workers (2021; 1,815 respondents) chose which of two news articles (headline and source: Fox News, MSNBC, USA Today) they would prefer to read over 12 pairs, randomly assigned to a forced-choice arm or an arm allowing 'Neither', then answered one repeated pair in the other format; a replication of Mummolo (2016).
Reference: Miller, D. R., & Ziegler, J. (2024). Preferential abstention in conjoint experiments. Research & Politics, 11(4).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/miller_2024_abstention.R (also builds miller_2024_scandal_candidates). New MTurk data, not the mummolo_2021_partisan_loyalty data. trial_arm = assigned arm, trial_format = format of the task (task 13 repeats task trial_repeat_of in the other format). Attribute row order recorded (attrpos_). MTurk confirmation codes, Qualtrics ResponseIds, IP flags and free text dropped.

Description: US MTurk workers (2021; 2,255 respondents) chose between and rated 6 pairs of hypothetical congressional candidates varying party, recent news (scandal or praise) and, depending on a randomized information environment, up to 8 further characteristics; respondents were assigned to a forced-choice arm or an arm allowing 'neither', and repeated task 1 in the other format; a replication of Funck & McCabe (2022).
Reference: Miller, D. R., & Ziegler, J. (2024). Preferential abstention in conjoint experiments. Research & Politics, 11(4).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/miller_2024_abstention.R (also builds miller_2024_news_selection). Characteristics not displayed in Moderate (3 shown) and Low (none shown) information environments are "(not shown)"; trial_info_environment records the environment. Party pair order set by survey block. Task 7 repeats task 1 in the other format. Ratings 1-5 agree. Gender and race levels are unequal (Male 66%, White 50%), undocumented. MTurk confirmation codes, Qualtrics ResponseIds, IP flags and free text dropped.

Description: Brazilian online-panel respondents (June 2022; n=2,008) chose between two foreign-investment projects (firm size, origin, entry mode, sales destination, jobs, salaries, corruption and environmental record) in 6 tasks, once for the good of their state and once for themselves and their family.
Reference: Moehlecke, C., Fasolin, G. N., & Spektor, M. (2025). Beyond jobs: When citizens reject socially irresponsible foreign direct investment. International Studies Quarterly, 69(3), sqaf046.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/moehlecke_2025.R. Two outcomes (choice_state = sociotropic, choice_family = egotropic) as described in the authors' code; exact Portuguese wording not deposited and the article is paywalled. Fixed design: 20 versions (trial_version), each fixing all 6 pairs; 223 of 960 possible profiles occur. Attribute text Portuguese as displayed. Panel member IDs, city and IBGE municipality codes dropped.

Description: Respondents (n=386) chose which of two hypothetical art-museum visits they preferred, varying featured artist, exhibition description, event, program, ticket cost and location; 6 pairs each.
Reference: Mohr, Z., Olivares, A., & Piatak, J. (2024). Are public spaces welcoming to all? A conjoint experiment on cultural representation and inclusionary practices in museums. Public Administration, 102(3), 841-859.
Notes: data/conjoint/mohr_2024.R. Attribute text is the authors' short Stata labels (exhibition description 'Juxtaposing' / 'Black men' was longer on screen); question wording not deposited; article not reachable, so sample source, country and N not checked. One unanswered task dropped.

Description: German voting-eligible adults from the Payback Online Panel, May/June 2018 (amended-design arm, n=1,714), chose between 5 pairs of fictitious candidates without party labels, varying positions on euro-area cooperation, social housing, tariffs and referendums and a first and second policy priority. Outcome: which candidate they would rather vote for.
Reference: Neuner, F. G., & Wratil, C. (2022). The populist marketplace: Unpacking the role of "thin" and "thick" ideology. Political Behavior, 44(2), 551-574.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2022.R. Task/profile inferred from row order (A/B alternation, as in the authors' own task analysis). German level text from Stata labels. Amended arm of the 2018 sample; the other half is neuner_2022_populist_candidates_2018.

Description: German voting-eligible adults from the Payback Online Panel, 2017 (third panel wave, n=2,371), chose between 5 pairs of fictitious candidates without party labels, varying positions on refugees, the EU, taxes on the rich and free trade and a first and second policy priority. Outcome: which candidate they would rather vote for.
Reference: Neuner, F. G., & Wratil, C. (2022). The populist marketplace: Unpacking the role of "thin" and "thick" ideology. Political Behavior, 44(2), 551-574.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2022.R. Task/profile inferred from row order (A/B alternation, as in the authors' own task analysis). German level text from Stata labels.

Description: German voting-eligible adults from the Payback Online Panel, May/June 2018 (exact-replication arm, n=1,712), chose between 5 pairs of fictitious candidates without party labels, varying positions on refugees, the EU, taxes on the rich and free trade and a first and second policy priority. Outcome: which candidate they would rather vote for.
Reference: Neuner, F. G., & Wratil, C. (2022). The populist marketplace: Unpacking the role of "thin" and "thick" ideology. Political Behavior, 44(2), 551-574.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2022.R. Task/profile inferred from row order (A/B alternation, as in the authors' own task analysis). German level text from Stata labels. Replication arm of the 2018 sample; the other half is neuner_2022_populist_amended_2018.

Description: Adults in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain (IPSOS opt-in panels, November 2022; n=3,839) chose between two hypothetical European security pacts (goal, financing, governance, opt-outs, joint purchases, size) and rated each on a 5-point scale; 3 pairs each, military-framing arm.
Reference: Nicoli, F., Burgoon, B., & van der Duin, D. (2025). Citizen support for a European Defense Union: An international conjoint experiment on security cooperation in Europe. International Studies Quarterly, 69(3), sqaf044.
Notes: data/conjoint/nicoli_2025.R. Attribute text is the article's English Table 1 mapped from the authors' Stata labels; respondents saw national-language versions (not deposited). Military arm only; the energy-security arm in the same deposit is not built (its attribute text is not documented). Article reports 750 per country (3,750); file has 3,839; authors' main sample = cov_attention_pass 1 (2,893).

Description: 1,021 Danish YouGov panel respondents (2 x 5 pairs) compared hypothetical Folketing candidates varying gender, age, occupation, party and three kinds of localism (where raised/lives, time spent on local issues, local visibility); outcomes are a 1-5 likelihood of voting for each candidate and a preferred-candidate choice with a don't-know option.
Reference: Nyholt, N. (2024). Why do voters prefer local candidates? Evidence from a Danish conjoint survey experiment. Political Behavior, 46, 2313-2332.
Notes: data/conjoint/nyholt_2024.R. Danish level text from Stata value labels, truncated at 80 characters for 5 long localism levels. Behavioral/symbolic localism "(not shown)" = omitted by design. Rating reversed to 5 = very likely. All 1,021 kept; the authors drop 242 speeders (cov_total_time). Survey weight kept.

Description: Adults in 12 rural Malawian constituencies (face-to-face, 2022; n=2,233) chose which of two hypothetical MP candidates (gender, party, policy focus, education, profession) they would vote for and which others in their constituency would vote for, 6 pairs each, after a randomized voter-education or control video.
Reference: Ofosu, G. K., Seeberg, M. B., & Wahman, M. (2026). Messages matter: How voter education campaigns affect citizens' willingness to vote for women. Journal of Politics, 88(1), 145-161.
Notes: data/conjoint/ofosu_2026.R. Attribute text = codebook English labels; levels were read aloud with visual symbols. Party levels Independent/Minor/Major stand for constituency-specific party names (2019 winner = Major, runner-up = Minor) not deposited. trial_video: Control / Low viability (= discrimination campaign) / High viability (= progress campaign). Pilot interviews dropped; 6 of the paper's 2,239 have no answers. Enumerator names and free text dropped.

Description: YouGov MENA panel respondents in Egypt (August 2019; n=1,028: 1,000 Egyptians plus 28 expats) made 5 forced choices between two systems of government varying elections, barriers to participation, official religion, the role of religious leaders, public-service provision and unemployment.
Reference: Ridge, H. M. (2024). Democratic commitment in the Middle East: A conjoint analysis. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(2), 285-300.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ridge_2024.R (one script, two country tables, separate fieldings analysed separately). Non-nationals kept and flagged by cov_nationality (the author excludes them; nationals match the article). About 94% answered in Arabic; level text is the English version (Arabic text not deposited; the article says the English is not a translation of the Arabic). Dropped 3 tasks with no choice and 3 with two chosen profiles (data errors).

Description: YouGov MENA panel respondents in Morocco (January 2020; n=1,009: 991 Moroccans plus 18 expats) made 5 forced choices between two systems of government varying elections, barriers to participation, official religion, the role of religious leaders, public-service provision and unemployment.
Reference: Ridge, H. M. (2024). Democratic commitment in the Middle East: A conjoint analysis. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(2), 285-300.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ridge_2024.R (one script, two country tables, separate fieldings analysed separately). Non-nationals kept and flagged by cov_nationality (the author excludes them; nationals match the article). About 94% answered in Arabic; level text is the English version (Arabic text not deposited; the article says the English is not a translation of the Arabic). Dropped 1 task with no choice and 1 with two chosen profiles (data errors).

Description: US adults (YouGov opt-in panel, June-August 2023; 2,334 respondents) compared 4 pairs of hypothetical strategies for supporting Ukraine varying casualties, destroyed infrastructure, US military and economic aid, nuclear risk, territorial cessions and Ukrainian self-determination; they chose one strategy per pair and rated each strategy (1-7, reject to support) in 2 of the 4 pairs.
Reference: Rudolph, L. (2026). Is there a partisan divide in citizens' preferences on Ukraine support? Survey-experimental evidence from the US. Public Opinion Quarterly.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/rudolph_2026.R. Level text is the author's short English labels (do-file); the aid attributes displayed a dollar amount plus GDP share, only the share survives. Rating reversed for the reversed-scale half as in the author's code (trial_scale_reversed). trial_task_no is the source's task-number identifier (round order); task is the screen index.

Description: Tunisian municipal-election candidates (LECS, April-May 2018; n=1,896 answering) chose which of two hypothetical aspirants they would first invite onto their list (party affiliation, sex, age, background, profession; Arabic text); 3 pairs each, forced choice.
Reference: Sasmaz, A. (2026). Organizational cohesion and unequal political selection: Evidence from Tunisia's secular-Islamist competition. Perspectives on Politics, 1-23.
Notes: data/conjoint/sasmaz_2026.R. Attribute levels are the Arabic text shown; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_ from source column order). Fielded levels differ from the English questionnaire (ages 25/33/41/49/57; 'public-sector job' where the form says Lawyer, which the author's code labels 'lawyer'). Paper's conjoint analyses use Nidaa/Ennahda party members only.

Description: US college students (203 respondents) chose between and rated 10 pairs of hypothetical roommates varying race, sexual orientation, religion, party, political interest, cleanliness, music, hobby, social life, values and bedtime.
Reference: Shafranek, R. M. (2021). Political considerations in nonpolitical decisions: A conjoint analysis of roommate choice. Political Behavior, 43(1), 271-300.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/shafranek_2021.R. Task and profile are inferred from row order (verified: exactly one chosen per inferred pair); task order assumed. Outcome wording unknown (article paywalled, no questionnaire deposited). LGBT level weighted 1/5 by design. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed; 2 respondents with no attribute values dropped.

Description: 1,817 Brazilian adults recruited by Facebook ads (May 2019) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical federal deputy candidates varying sex, age, education, occupation, experience, religion (Catholic/Evangelical) and abortion, economic and security policy stances.
Reference: Smith, A. E., & Boas, T. C. (2023). Religion, sexuality politics, and the transformation of Latin American electorates. British Journal of Political Science, 54, 816-835.
Notes: data/conjoint/smith_2023.R. One table per country (Brazil/Chile/Peru, separate fieldings and languages). 9 binary attributes; abortion levels are keep current laws vs complete ban (legalization not offered). trial_order = policy block first or last. Authors' eligibility filter applied; N matches the article. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: 3,732 Chilean adults recruited by Facebook ads (May 2019) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical diputado candidates varying sex, age, education, occupation, experience, religion (Catholic/Evangelical) and abortion, economic and security policy stances.
Reference: Smith, A. E., & Boas, T. C. (2023). Religion, sexuality politics, and the transformation of Latin American electorates. British Journal of Political Science, 54, 816-835.
Notes: data/conjoint/smith_2023.R. One table per country (Brazil/Chile/Peru, separate fieldings and languages). 9 binary attributes; abortion levels are keep current laws vs complete ban (legalization not offered). trial_order = policy block first or last. Authors' eligibility filter applied; N matches the article. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: 3,698 Peruvian adults recruited by Facebook ads (May 2019) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical congressional candidates varying sex, age, education, occupation, experience, religion (Catholic/Evangelical) and abortion, economic and security policy stances.
Reference: Smith, A. E., & Boas, T. C. (2023). Religion, sexuality politics, and the transformation of Latin American electorates. British Journal of Political Science, 54, 816-835.
Notes: data/conjoint/smith_2023.R. One table per country (Brazil/Chile/Peru, separate fieldings and languages). 9 binary attributes; abortion levels are keep current laws vs complete ban (legalization not offered). trial_order = policy block first or last. Authors' eligibility filter applied; N matches the article. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: Dutch adults (Dynata, Feb-Mar 2019, n=3,246) compared two hypothetical neighbourhood participatory budgets (who can submit, which projects, municipal support, who picks the winner); 6 pairs each, forced choice plus a 1-7 approval rating of each budget.
Reference: van der Does, R., & Kantorowicz, J. (2022). Political exclusion and support for democratic innovations: Evidence from a conjoint experiment on participatory budgeting. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(4), 947-955.
Notes: data/conjoint/vanderdoes_2022.R. The fifth randomized attribute (winning project shown) is not deposited; only the authors' derived respondent-specific favorability is, and it is dropped. Attribute text = authors' English labels; attribute order randomized but not recorded. Footnote 7 minority difference (+3.9pp) reproduced.

Description: US adults (CloudResearch, February 2024; 2,052 respondents with ratings) saw 3 pairs of hypothetical Congressional candidates' Twitter profiles ending in an uncivil attack, varying party, gender (name and photo), leadership traits, insider status, attack type, issue, insult vs ridicule and incivility context; each attack was rated 0-100 on impoliteness, unacceptability, abnormality and wrongness, and each candidate on a 0-100 feeling thermometer.
Reference: Vargiu, C., Nai, A., & Garzia, D. (2026). Incivility does not exist: An experimental assessment on the drivers of incivility perceptions and their effects on candidate evaluations. The Journal of Politics, 88(2), 867-881.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vargiu_2026.R. Levels are the authors' labels; the displayed tweet text (Appendix A) differs slightly between profile A and B. Gender is conveyed only by first name and photo. Which of three insult/ridicule texts was shown is not saved, only the type. Perception ratings are kept as asked (higher = more uncivil); rating = feeling thermometer. cov_in_authors_sample reproduces the report's n = 1,884 (1,843 with ratings).

Description: US YouGov respondents who use Facebook or Twitter (2022, n=500) chose between two hypothetical Members of Congress in 10 text (box) conjoint tasks varying 9 attributes. Outcome: which candidate they would rather have as their Representative.
Reference: Vecchiato, A., & Munger, K. (2025). Introducing the visual conjoint, with an application to candidate evaluation on social media. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12(1), 57-71.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vecchiato_2025.R. Same respondents also did the visual conjoint (vecchiato_2025_candidates_visual). Article says 5 tasks per respondent, data have 10. YouGov caseids re-keyed; free-text fields dropped.

Description: US YouGov respondents who use Facebook or Twitter (2022, n=500) chose between two hypothetical Members of Congress shown as mock Twitter profiles (photo, bio, follower and like counts, two partisan tweets) in 10 tasks varying 9 attributes. Outcome: which candidate they would rather have as their Representative.
Reference: Vecchiato, A., & Munger, K. (2025). Introducing the visual conjoint, with an application to candidate evaluation on social media. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12(1), 57-71.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vecchiato_2025.R. Image conjoint: attr_ levels are the authors' Table 1 labels decoded from the displayed image file names (race shown only by photo; gender by photo and Congressman/Congresswoman title; feedback by follower/like counts). Tweet-variant codes dropped (tweet text not deposited). The authors' image.RData mis-codes profession for 919 profiles; file names used. 8 skipped tasks omitted.

Description: 8,279 Kantar panel respondents in Germany, Italy, Romania and Sweden (July 2022) compared 4 pairs of fictitious activist Twitter profiles varying gender, age, an issue claim (pro/anti climate, immigration, taxation) and a personality cue (narcissism/agreeableness); outcomes are which profile made them feel more represented and a 1-7 rating of feeling represented by each.
Reference: Vik, A., de Wilde, P., Treib, O., & Aaroe, L. (2025). Venturing beyond the vote: Routes to feeling represented through unelected representation. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e102.
Notes: data/conjoint/vik_2025.R. Four countries pooled (cov_country) as in the article. attr_ values are the authors' level names, not displayed text (gender/age shown by name and photo; issue and personality by tweets in the national language). 100 pre-drawn design versions (trial_version); level shares unequal and attributes dependent. Survey weight kept.

Description: 928 non-Hispanic white US adults (Lucid, December 2021) each rated about 20 single profiles of hypothetical immigrants (age, gender, race/ethnicity, years in the US, English, education, government benefits, police record) on how likely the person is to be an illegal/undocumented immigrant (0-10).
Reference: Zhirkov, K., & Van De Hey, L. (2025). Multidimensional constructions of target groups and their political implications: The case of immigrant (il)legality. PS: Political Science & Politics, 58(4), 641-650.
Notes: data/conjoint/zhirkov_2025_target_groups.R. Single-profile tasks (profile = 1). Rating is perceived likelihood of being undocumented (not favourability). 928 of the article's 935 respondents have conjoint rows. Police record and benefits are yes/no at 1/2, 'yes' split across specific levels.

Description: US adults (Bovitz, September 2022) chose between two refugee profiles described by 7 attributes (reason for leaving incl. climate-caused disaster or poverty, origin, children, English skills, gender, age, religion). 1,117 respondents, 5 paired tasks; two forced choices per task: who should receive the visa and who would integrate more successfully.
Reference: Adman, P., Lajevardi, N., & Seligsohn, D. (2024). American attitudes toward climate migrants: Findings from a conjoint experiment. PS: Political Science & Politics, 57(4).
Notes: data/conjoint/adman_2024.R. Two outcome columns (visa choice, integration choice). The article reports 5,175 profile pairs, but the deposit has 1,117 x 5 = 5,585. Respondent covariates limited to gender (authors' dummies), birth year and age; the other survey codes have no labels.

Description: Chilean adults in a Netquest online panel (wave 2, Nov-Dec 2021, n = 3,075) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical presidential candidates varying on 6 attributes (ideology, gender, age, feminism, immigration and crime proposals); outcome is which candidate they would choose, with a 'neither' option.
Reference: Argote, P., & Visconti, G. (2025). Causes and consequences of ideological persistence: The case of Chile. Latin American Politics and Society, 67, 80-103.
Notes: data/conjoint/argote_2025.R. Levels are the authors' English short labels of Spanish display text. 'Ninguno' (neither) in 6,184 of 15,375 tasks, coded 0/0 (authors drop them). Article text says ages 35-65 and 'first wave'; data and appendix have ages 40/50/60 and wave 2. Two survey weights kept (cell and rake).

Description: US adults (YouGov, June 2014, n = 2,250) chose between 8 pairs of hypothetical federal income tax plans varying in the marginal rate for six income brackets and, for 2,000 respondents, the plan's total revenue relative to today; outcome is the preferred plan.
Reference: Ballard-Rosa, C., Martin, L., & Scheve, K. (2017). The structure of American income tax policy preferences. The Journal of Politics, 79(1), 1-16.
Notes: data/conjoint/ballardrosa_2017.R. Levels are the .dta value labels; bracket names from the authors' labels. 250 respondents in the no-revenue arm have attr_revenue '(not shown)' (trial_saw_revenue = 0); the authors' main analyses use the 2,000 others. Question wording not in the deposit. Same data as cregg::taxes and the ARHZU4 re-host.

Description: Moroccan survey respondents (n = 927) each evaluated 6 hypothetical politician (MP) profiles one at a time, varying on 7 attributes (gender, party, education, character, legislative productivity, policy priorities, family status); outcomes are whether they would re-elect the politician and a 1-10 competence rating.
Reference: Barnett, C., Blackman, A., & Shalaby, M. (2025). Gender stereotypes in autocracies: Experimental evidence from Morocco. The Journal of Politics, 87(3), 995-1011.
Notes: data/conjoint/barnett_2025.R. CC BY-NC 4.0 (Ben ruled 10-07 NC acceptable for conj). Levels are the authors' English factor labels; display language and outcome wording not deposited (codebook descriptions). Single-profile design; reelect stored as choice with opt-out. Derived indices dropped.

Description: Moroccan face-to-face respondents (n = 873, 2023) compared 4 pairs of hypothetical parliamentary candidates on 7 attributes including gender, saying which they prefer, which men and which women in their community would prefer, and rating each candidate's competence 1-10.
Reference: Barnett, C., Blackman, A., & Shalaby, M. (2026). Misperceptions of male bias against female candidates: An obstacle to women's political representation? Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/barnett_2026.R. CC BY-NC 4.0 (Ben ruling 10-07). Article DOI not yet in Crossref. Level text is the authors' English labels; outcome wording paraphrased from the codebook. Same survey programme as barnett_2025_politicians_morocco (different conjoint).

Description: US online respondents (Lucid/Qualtrics, October 2019; n = 4,334, 4,042 completing all pairs) read a hypothetical employment-discrimination case (type randomized across 5 arms) and compared 5 pairs of judges varying on 7 attributes (race, gender, sexual orientation, nominating party, age, law school, previous job); outcomes are which judge they trust more to hear the case fairly, plus 1-7 ideology and impartiality placements and 1-4 trust in the Supreme Court if the judge joined it.
Reference: Bracic, A., Israel-Trummel, M., Johnson, T., & Tipler, K. (2023). "Because he is gay": How race, gender, and sexuality shape perceptions of judicial fairness. The Journal of Politics, 85(4), 1167-1181.
Notes: data/conjoint/bracic_2023.R. Raw Qualtrics export with displayed level text; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Partial respondents kept (authors analyse the 4,042 who completed 5 pairs). Ideology and court-trust ratings stored as codebook option codes. IP, GPS, zip, Lucid rid and free text dropped.

Description: British YouGov respondents (December 2012; n=1,899) each made 5 forced choices between two hypothetical MPs varying in party, tenure, days spent on constituency work, how often the MP speaks out or votes against the party leadership, and sex (pronoun).
Reference: Campbell, R., Cowley, P., Vivyan, N., & Wagner, M. (2019). Legislator dissent as a valence signal. British Journal of Political Science, 49(1), 105-128.
Notes: data/conjoint/campbell_2019_dissent.R (Study 2). Level text is the bold level from the article's Figure 1 screenshot (party, tenure, constituency days, dissent frequency, He/She), not the full sentences. Profile (MP 1/2) is inferred from row order within task. Authors' respondent-by-MP derived variables dropped; qual kept as codes (no labels in the deposit).

Description: British YouGov respondents (September 2013; n=1,919) each made 5 forced choices between two hypothetical MPs varying in party, days spent on constituency work, whether the MP mainly follows own or constituents' views, how publicly the MP voices dissent from the party leadership, and sex (pronoun).
Reference: Campbell, R., Cowley, P., Vivyan, N., & Wagner, M. (2019). Legislator dissent as a valence signal. British Journal of Political Science, 49(1), 105-128.
Notes: data/conjoint/campbell_2019_dissent.R (Study 3). Motivation and dissent-type text is the article's quoted wording mapped from the authors' short labels; the full profile sentences are not reproduced in the article. Profile (MP 1/2) is inferred from row order within task. qual kept as codes (no labels in the deposit).

Description: Paraguayan respondents compared pairs of street-level bureaucrats described by 6 attributes (took bribes, diverted public funds, gender, party, age, education). 3,107 respondents, 5 paired tasks, three forced-choice outcomes per pair whose wording is not in the deposit.
Reference: Carreras, M., Vera, S., & Visconti, G. (2024). Gender stereotypes and petty corruption among street-level bureaucrats: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Research & Politics, 11(3).
Notes: data/conjoint/carreras_2024.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (verified: 10 contiguous rows per respondent, one chosen per pair on all three outcomes). choice = the authors' main outcome (outcome_q3); choice_q1/choice_q2 = their alternative outcomes; no wording in the deposit and the article could not be retrieved. Attribute text is the authors' English translation.

Description: Chinese SSI respondents (February 2015; n=1,613) read five vignettes about a foreign company trying to acquire a Chinese company, varying ownership, firm size, economic distress and the home country's reciprocity policy, and said whether the Chinese government should prevent the transaction.
Reference: Chilton, A. S., Milner, H. V., & Tingley, D. (2020). Reciprocity and public opposition to foreign direct investment. British Journal of Political Science, 50(1), 129-153.
Notes: data/conjoint/chilton_2020.R (China primary experiment). Single-profile yes/no vignettes; choice = 1 Yes (prevent). Level text is the authors' short English labels (Chinese display text not deposited). Task order inferred from row order; three ids with 10 rows dropped. No covariates.

Description: US SSI respondents (February 2015; n=2,003) read five vignettes about a foreign company trying to acquire an American company, varying ownership, home country, national-security risk, firm size, economic distress and the home country's reciprocity policy, and said whether the US government should prevent the transaction.
Reference: Chilton, A. S., Milner, H. V., & Tingley, D. (2020). Reciprocity and public opposition to foreign direct investment. British Journal of Political Science, 50(1), 129-153.
Notes: data/conjoint/chilton_2020.R (US primary experiment). Single-profile yes/no vignettes; choice = 1 Yes (prevent). Task order inferred from row order (no task column). One id with 10 rows dropped. No covariates (demographics file has no respondent id). Wording from the Cambridge supplementary materials.

Description: 1,008 Egyptian adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, Sep 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position).

Description: 1,022 Indian adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, Sep 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position). Respondents chose Hindi or English (cov_survey_language) but the export stores the attribute text in Hindi only; one respondent-wealth level has two Unicode spellings (as stored; the authors merge them).

Description: 1,047 Italian adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, Sep 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position).

Description: 1,012 Japanese adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, Sep 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position). In Japan an administrative error showed respondents drawn for 'somewhat dangerous' or 'very dangerous' both descriptors in one level (stored as displayed; public safety has 3 levels).

Description: 1,037 Thai adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, Sep 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position).

Description: 1,024 US adults (Qualtrics panel with quotas, May 2023) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical countries varying 10 attributes (leader selection, civil liberties, leader constraints, corruption, national economy, own wealth, public safety, health care, minority treatment, own group status) on where they would prefer to be born and grow up, and rated each country 1-7 on how happy they would be to have grown up there.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2025). Are people willing to trade away democracy for desirable outcomes? Experimental evidence from six countries. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2025.R (six country tables; the authors pool them after translating levels, but the displayed text is in six languages). Attribute order randomized per respondent; only the democracy block position (top/middle/bottom) is recorded (trial_democracy_position).

Description: 1,013 US adults (NORC AmeriSpeak, March-April 2021) each judged which of two mock-up online ads was more political, over 8 pairs; ads varied the sponsor (6), the energy/environment message (6) and the image (5).
Reference: Edelson, L., Lockett, D., Guillard, C., Lauinger, T., Li, Z., Montgomery, J. M., & McCoy, D. (2025). What drives perceptions of the political in online advertising? The source, content, and political orientation. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 13(1), 36-50.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/edelson_2025.R. Image conjoint: attr_ are the authors' labels of each ad's sponsor, message and image, not displayed text (ads were pictures). 96 unanswered tasks dropped. Real-ads experiment in the deposit not built (single manipulated factor).

Description: 3,000 news-engaged US registered voters (YouGov, January 2024) each read 8 text descriptions of a city-council seat varying 7 features (campaign funds needed, chances of winning, salary, local news exposure, majority needed to pass policy, city manager powers, staff) and rated their interest in running for it on a 1-10 scale.
Reference: Eggers, A., Fowler, A., Howell, W., & Offer-Westort, M. (2025). Opportunities to govern: How to increase the supply of moderate and qualified candidates. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/eggers_2025.R. Single-profile text vignette; attr_ = displayed sentence (bold tags removed), sentence order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Rating stored raw 1-10 (authors rescale to 0-1). Question wording not deposited. Includes YouGov weight. Codebook is inside PSRM.zip (UCHI0012_codebook.pdf).

Description: 3,037 Facebook-recruited Ukrainian adults (2020, survey in Ukrainian or Russian) compared 4 pairs of healthcare (Petro hurt his leg; doctor Ruslana announces a long wait at a state clinic) scenarios varying 11 attributes (wait time, need, substitutes, bribe size, detection risk, enforceability, past/future interaction, other bribers, first mover, multiple officials) plus randomized citizen/official names; forced choice of the scenario where the citizen is more likely to bribe, and 1-7 ratings of the citizen's and the respondent's own likelihood of bribing.
Reference: Erlich, A., Gans-Morse, J., & Nichter, S. (2025). Selective bribery: When do citizens engage in corruption? Comparative Political Studies, 58(5), 996-1036.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/erlich_2025.R (both scenarios; one table each). Attribute text stored as displayed in the respondent's survey language (Ukrainian or Russian; see cov_survey_language), so each level has two spellings. Ratings exported as Russian answer text, mapped 1 = definitely no ... 7 = definitely yes (authors' code numbers them the other way and reverses before analysis). Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. GPS coordinates and panel IDs in the raw file dropped.

Description: 3,031 Facebook-recruited Ukrainian adults (2020, survey in Ukrainian or Russian) compared 4 pairs of driver's licence (Nina wants a licence; instructor Ivan announces a long wait) scenarios varying 11 attributes (wait time, need, substitutes, bribe size, detection risk, enforceability, past/future interaction, other bribers, first mover, multiple officials) plus randomized citizen/official names; forced choice of the scenario where the citizen is more likely to bribe, and 1-7 ratings of the citizen's and the respondent's own likelihood of bribing.
Reference: Erlich, A., Gans-Morse, J., & Nichter, S. (2025). Selective bribery: When do citizens engage in corruption? Comparative Political Studies, 58(5), 996-1036.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/erlich_2025.R (both scenarios; one table each). Attribute text stored as displayed in the respondent's survey language (Ukrainian or Russian; see cov_survey_language), so each level has two spellings. Ratings exported as Russian answer text, mapped 1 = definitely no ... 7 = definitely yes (authors' code numbers them the other way and reverses before analysis). Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. GPS coordinates and panel IDs in the raw file dropped.

Description: US CCES team-module respondents (n=823) each saw 4 single hypothetical candidates varying in gender, family, religion, military service, occupation and three issue priorities, guessed each candidate's ideology (liberal or conservative), said how sure they were, and rated the candidate 0-10.
Reference: Goggin, S. N., Henderson, J. A., & Theodoridis, A. G. (2020). What goes with red and blue? Mapping partisan and ideological associations in the minds of voters. Political Behavior, 42(4), 985-1013.
Notes: data/conjoint/goggin_2020.R (ideology experiment, JAH module; same people as the JAH half of goggin_2020_party_guess). 177 of 1,000 respondents have no ideology profiles saved and are dropped. Task order inferred from row order. rating_conservative 1 Conservative, 0 Liberal; rating_sure 1-4 from answer text. Wording not in the deposit.

Description: US CCES team-module respondents (n=2,000) each saw 4 single hypothetical candidates varying in gender, family, religion, military service, occupation and three issue priorities, guessed each candidate's party, said how sure they were, and rated the candidate 0-10.
Reference: Goggin, S. N., Henderson, J. A., & Theodoridis, A. G. (2020). What goes with red and blue? Mapping partisan and ideological associations in the minds of voters. Political Behavior, 42(4), 985-1013.
Notes: data/conjoint/goggin_2020.R (party experiment, two CCES modules pooled). rating_republican = party guess (1 Republican, 0 Democrat); rating_sure 1-4 coded from answer text; favorability 0-10. Question wording and CCES year not in the deposit (article not read). ZIP codes and free-text race dropped.

Description: German adults (YouGov quota sample, December 2020, n = 2,039) compared 6 pairs of hypothetical deliberative citizen forums varying on 9 attributes (issue, initiative, recruitment, size, composition, output, consensus, discussion format, authorization); outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-7 liking rating of each forum.
Reference: Goldberg, S., & Bächtiger, A. (2023). Catching the 'deliberative wave'? How (disaffected) citizens assess deliberative citizen forums. British Journal of Political Science, 53(1), 239-247.
Notes: data/conjoint/goldberg_2023.R. Attribute levels are the authors' English factor labels (display was German). Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. Article says sample weighted; no weight deposited. Derived outcome-favourability flag dropped; undocumented respondent items dropped.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n = 9,907) each chose which of two hypothetical immigrants (one college-educated, one with no formal education; profession, origin, reason and prior trips varied) they would admit, with contexts assigned by an adaptive bandit design plus two validation phases.
Reference: Gosciak, J., Molitor, D., & Lundberg, I. (2026). Adaptive randomization in conjoint survey experiments. Political Analysis, 1-28.
Notes: data/conjoint/gosciak_2026.R. One task per respondent; 16 context arms assigned adaptively (Thompson sampling), so level frequencies are very unequal (arm 7 and 10 dominate). Profile position inferred from option_preference and discriminated. Authors' exclusion flag kept as cov_garbage (9,146 non-garbage); 121 repeat submissions dropped.

Description: German panel respondents (September 2021) compared two COVID-19 restriction proposals varying in stringency and universality (3G/2G/all citizens) under a shared pandemic-severity scenario. 10,525 respondents, 2 paired tasks; outcomes: preferred proposal, 0-10 rating of each, trust in government (one random proposal) and, for the unvaccinated, likelihood of vaccinating.
Reference: Hartmann, F., Humphreys, M., Geissler, F., Kluever, H., & Giesecke, J. (2023). Trading liberties: Estimating COVID-19 policy preferences from conjoint data. Political Analysis.
Notes: data/conjoint/hartmann_2023.R. Severity is shared by both proposals of a task (a background attribute) and differs between the two tasks. Policy levels are the deposit's short German vignette labels; the full vignette text is not deposited. Keeps the 141 respondents the authors drop for a trust-outcome programming error (their rating_trust set to NA, flag in cov_pr_error_exp7) and the 14 with unknown vaccination status. Ratings kept 0-10 (authors divide by 10).

Description: Duke lab participants (eye-tracking, July 2019; n=122) each made 120 presidential vote choices in six blocks of 20 tasks, between 2 or 3 hypothetical candidates showing 5, 8 or 11 of 11 attributes (party and gender always shown).
Reference: Jenke, L., Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., & Hangartner, D. (2021). Using eye-tracking to understand decision-making in conjoint experiments. Political Analysis, 29(1), 75-101.
Notes: data/conjoint/jenke_2021.R. Built from the per-subject raw files: attributes a block did not show are '(not shown)' (shown set and row order from the `order` variable; matches the authors' NA pattern); attrpos_ = table row. 11 trials without valid fixations (dropped from the authors' eye-tracking analysis) kept with trial_fixation_data = 0. Codebook age level 36 vs article Table 1 37 (codebook kept). Re-hosted Bansak et al. 2019 data not built.

Description: 1,786 Denmark adults (YouGov DK, Dec 2018) each judged 4 political statements whose timing, sender (Venstre, Socialdemokratiet, Dansk Folkeparti, Radikale Venstre, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, Mette Frederiksen), commitment wording, numeric goal, policy content, time horizon and condition were randomized; outcomes: is it an election pledge (yes/no), should the sender be held accountable (yes/no), and 1-5 ratings of priority, sender's ability to act, and impossibility of checking.
Reference: Krishnarajan, S., & Jensen, C. (2022). When is a pledge a pledge? British Journal of Political Science, 52(4), 1911-1922.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krishnarajan_2022.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Single-statement text vignettes, task = statement 1-4, profile = 1. Omitted numeric goal / time horizon / condition clauses are '(not shown)'. Don't know on outcomes = NA. Respondents: 1,800 in the deposit (appendix C1: 2,031); respondents with no answered outcome dropped.

Description: 2,038 Britain adults (YouGov GB, Dec 2018) each judged 4 political statements whose timing, sender (Conservatives, Labour, UKIP, Liberal Democrats, Theresa May, Jeremy Corbyn), commitment wording, numeric goal, policy content, time horizon and condition were randomized; outcomes: is it an election pledge (yes/no), should the sender be held accountable (yes/no), and 1-5 ratings of priority, sender's ability to act, and impossibility of checking.
Reference: Krishnarajan, S., & Jensen, C. (2022). When is a pledge a pledge? British Journal of Political Science, 52(4), 1911-1922.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krishnarajan_2022.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Single-statement text vignettes, task = statement 1-4, profile = 1. Omitted numeric goal / time horizon / condition clauses are '(not shown)'. Don't know on outcomes = NA. Respondents: 2,050 in the deposit (appendix C1: 2,214); respondents with no answered outcome dropped.

Description: 1,721 United States adults (YouGov US, Feb 2019) each judged 4 political statements whose timing, sender (Republicans, Democrats, Donald Trump, Nancy Pelosi), commitment wording, numeric goal, policy content, time horizon and condition were randomized; outcomes: is it an election pledge (yes/no), should the sender be held accountable (yes/no), and 1-5 ratings of priority, sender's ability to act, and impossibility of checking.
Reference: Krishnarajan, S., & Jensen, C. (2022). When is a pledge a pledge? British Journal of Political Science, 52(4), 1911-1922.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krishnarajan_2022.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Single-statement text vignettes, task = statement 1-4, profile = 1. Omitted numeric goal / time horizon / condition clauses are '(not shown)'. Don't know on outcomes = NA. Respondents: 1,745 in the deposit (appendix C1: 2,032); respondents with no answered outcome dropped.

Description: White, Black, Asian and Hispanic US respondents (n = 786, Qualtrics panel, 2016) made 10 vote choices between two hypothetical candidates varying in race (including six multiracial combinations), gender, party, ideology, nativity and experience.
Reference: Lemi, D. C. (2021). Do voters prefer just any descriptive representative? The case of multiracial candidates. Perspectives on Politics, 19(4), 1061-1081.
Notes: data/conjoint/lemi_2020.R. Author's exclusions already applied in the deposit (786 = article N). Outcome wording paraphrased (no conjoint questionnaire in deposit). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). 6 unanswered tasks omitted.

Description: 502 Romanian eligible voters (non-probability sample in 30 localities, 2016, before the local elections) each chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical mayoral candidates described by 7 attributes: gender, incumbency, corruption investigation, vote buying, threats to non-supporters, policy pledges and income. Outcome: vote choice, with a neither option.
Reference: Mares, I., & Visconti, G. (2020). Voting for the lesser evil: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Romania. Political Science Research and Methods, 8(2), 315-328.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mares_2020.R. Attribute text is the English text of the online appendix Table A1 (survey language not stated). selected = 3 (257 tasks) undocumented; treated as 'neither' since the authors code both candidates 0. Each pair has one incumbent and one non-incumbent by design. Ethnicity, income and party kept as unlabelled codes.

Description: Adults in England (n=1,286) each made 6 forced choices between two policy packages varying mortgage and credit-card interest rates, social assistance, unemployment insurance duration and income tax.
Reference: Markgraf, J., & Rosas, G. (2024). Borrowing to self-insure? Credit access and support for welfare. The Journal of Politics, 86(2), 642-655.
Notes: data/conjoint/markgraf_2024.R. cleanedConjointData.csv is a gzip R data file, not a CSV. Profile (1/2) is order of appearance in a shuffled file and carries no position information. Question wording, survey firm and dates not in the deposit (article not read). Covariates are the authors' coded variables. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: YouGov respondents in Denmark, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Romania and the UK (Feb-Mar 2022; n=10,347) each made 5 forced choices between two hypothetical parliamentary candidates varying in institutional and extra-institutional experience, reason for running, and migration and climate positions, and rated each candidate 1-7.
Reference: Mercea, D., & Santos, F. G. (2025). Policy over protest: Experimental evidence on the drivers of support for movement parties. Perspectives on Politics, 23(3), 901-923.
Notes: data/conjoint/mercea_2025.R. Six countries pooled with cov_country as in the authors' main analysis. Level text is the English instrument (UK labels; two SPSS-truncated labels completed from article Table 2; migration levels carry '[COUNTRY]'), not the national display text, which the .sav files hold truncated at 120 bytes. Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded.

Description: Japanese online respondents (n = 1,504) saw 3 pairs of hypothetical candidates described by agree/neither/disagree positions on 8 policy issues and, depending on a randomized label arm, picked the more right-wing or the more left-wing candidate and placed each on a 1-10 left-right scale.
Reference: Miwa, H., Arami, R., & Taniguchi, M. (2023). Detecting voter understanding of ideological labels using a conjoint experiment. Political Behavior, 45(2).
Notes: data/conjoint/miwa_2021.R. Attribute text in Japanese as displayed; issue order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Choice outcome split by label arm (choice_more_right / choice_more_left). Rating endpoint labels not in deposit; data imply higher = more right. Authors' satisficer and <=5 s task exclusions not applied (attention items and timing kept).

Description: US opt-in panel respondents (n = 623, August 2024) made 5 choices between two countries described by economic wellbeing, press freedom, presidential power/elections and rule of law, each at a normative, illiberal-majority or illiberal-minority level.
Reference: Mortenson, C., & Nisbet, E. (2025). Benefit seekers or principle holders? Experimental evidence on Americans' democratic trade-offs. Perspectives on Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/mortenson_2025.R. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Respondent covariates are unlabelled Qualtrics codes (_code). Source export holds IP addresses, GPS and panel ids (dropped).

Description: US Democrats and Republicans from the main sample (provider not stated in the deposit) (n = 1,059) made 12 choices between two news items, each a headline (11 topics x 3 wordings) attributed to Fox News, MSNBC or USA Today.
Reference: Mummolo, J. (2016). News from the other side: How topic relevance limits the prevalence of partisan selective exposure. The Journal of Politics, 78(3), 763-773.
Notes: data/conjoint/mummolo_2016.R. Wording paraphrased (article and questionnaire not accessible); trial_scheme and trial_rows are undocumented respondent-level design codes kept as stored; covariates are the author's 0/1 dummies. Second sample of the same design is mummolo_2016_news_choice_mturk.

Description: US Democrats and Republicans from an MTurk sample (n = 1,444) made 10 choices between two news items, each a headline (11 topics x 3 wordings) attributed to Fox News, MSNBC or USA Today.
Reference: Mummolo, J. (2016). News from the other side: How topic relevance limits the prevalence of partisan selective exposure. The Journal of Politics, 78(3), 763-773.
Notes: data/conjoint/mummolo_2016.R. Wording paraphrased (article and questionnaire not accessible); trial_scheme and trial_rows are undocumented respondent-level design codes kept as stored; covariates are the author's 0/1 dummies. Same design as mummolo_2016_news_choice, MTurk sample.

Description: 1,893 US Lucid respondents (January 2021) rated up to 30 single profiles of a hypothetical person (race, gender, marital status, number of children, immigration status, employment status, criminal record) on how typical the person is of welfare recipients, 0-10, under one of two instruction versions. The article analyses the 1,293 non-Hispanic white respondents.
Reference: Myers, C. D., Zhirkov, K., & Lunz Trujillo, K. (2024). Who is "on welfare"? Validating the use of conjoint experiments to measure stereotype content. Political Behavior, 46, 89-110.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/myers_2024.R. All respondents kept; filter cov_race/cov_hispanic (nhwhite) for the article's sample, on which Figure 2 reproduces exactly. trial_instruction_code = instruction version 1/2, wording not in the deposit. Earlier study than zhirkov_2025_welfare_stereotypes (same design, different sample).

Description: 690 UK Prolific respondents (sample 3, UK Prolific, party not shown) compared 6 pairs of hypothetical politicians described by randomized statements (people-centrism, anti-elitism, filler); four forced choices (which politician is more likely to say politicians should listen to the people / the political class is crooked / immigration should be reduced / is conservative) and four 1-5 ratings of each politician.
Reference: Neuner, F. G. (2025). Can (thin) populism be manipulated without manipulating host ideology? Evidence from a conjoint validation approach. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 1-15.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2025.R (samples 1, 2, 3 = tables us1, us2, uk). Statements are stored as displayed; the control level of people-centrism and anti-elitism (no statement) is '(not shown)', as is the party in samples 1 and 3. UK education/income/race kept as codes (authors' labels do not fit the codes); UK ideology end labels unavailable.

Description: 699 US Prolific respondents (sample 1, US Prolific, party not shown) compared 6 pairs of hypothetical politicians described by randomized statements (people-centrism, anti-elitism, filler); four forced choices (which politician is more likely to say politicians should listen to the people / the political class is crooked / immigration should be reduced / is conservative) and four 1-5 ratings of each politician.
Reference: Neuner, F. G. (2025). Can (thin) populism be manipulated without manipulating host ideology? Evidence from a conjoint validation approach. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 1-15.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2025.R (samples 1, 2, 3 = tables us1, us2, uk). Statements are stored as displayed; the control level of people-centrism and anti-elitism (no statement) is '(not shown)', as is the party in samples 1 and 3.

Description: 704 US Prolific respondents (sample 2, US Prolific, party (Democrat/Republican) shown) compared 6 pairs of hypothetical politicians described by randomized statements (people-centrism, anti-elitism, filler, party); four forced choices (which politician is more likely to say politicians should listen to the people / the political class is crooked / immigration should be reduced / is conservative) and four 1-5 ratings of each politician.
Reference: Neuner, F. G. (2025). Can (thin) populism be manipulated without manipulating host ideology? Evidence from a conjoint validation approach. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 1-15.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neuner_2025.R (samples 1, 2, 3 = tables us1, us2, uk). Statements are stored as displayed; the control level of people-centrism and anti-elitism (no statement) is '(not shown)', as is the party in samples 1 and 3.

Description: 2,686 adults in Osaka Prefecture, Japan (Rakuten Research online panel, November 2015) each chose between 4 pairs of hypothetical same-party House of Representatives candidates described by 7 attributes: sex, education, personality trait, issue specialization and positions on social, economic and military issues. Outcome: vote choice.
Reference: Ono, Y., & Yamada, M. (2020). Do voters prefer gender stereotypic candidates? Evidence from a conjoint survey experiment in Japan. Political Science Research and Methods, 8(3), 477-492.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ono_2020.R. Survey in Japanese; attribute text is the authors' English translation (working paper Table 1) substituted for the file's short labels. Pair-sex flag (context) dropped; respondent education only as the authors' BA/no-BA split.

Description: German party-convention delegates (CDU, SPD, FDP, Die LINKE, Greens) chose between two hypothetical candidates described by 10 attributes (age, gender, education, occupation, district nomination, legislative experience, membership length, intra-party ideology, party office, activity). 296 delegates, up to 5 paired tasks; forced choice.
Reference: Rehmert, J. (2022). Party elites' preferences in candidates: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Political Behavior, 44.
Notes: data/conjoint/rehmert_2022.R. Attribute levels are the German value labels of the .dta (age labels are bare numbers 30/45/65). Level shares are unequal and dependent (occupation by education, membership length by experience); the authors interact these pairs. 3 respondents did fewer than 5 tasks. Question wording not in the deposit.

Description: US adults (n = 2,500, early 2017) each rated 4 hypothetical Supreme Court nominee profiles one at a time, varying on 6 attributes (age, gender, race, law school, current position, abortion view), with a respondent-level elite-rhetoric arm; outcomes are 1-5 support for the nominee and trust in the nominee's impartiality.
Reference: Rogowski, J. C., & Stone, A. R. (2021). How political contestation over judicial nominations polarizes Americans' attitudes toward the Supreme Court. British Journal of Political Science, 51(3), 1251-1269.
Notes: data/conjoint/rogowski_2021.R. Attribute text is the authors' cjoint design list (numeric codes in the file); current-position level 4 is 'Think-tank' there but 'Chief counsel' in the authors' plots. Task inferred from row order. Additive legitimacy index dropped (items not deposited). cov_pid3 collapses Other/Not sure into Independent.

Description: Argentine respondents near the age-18 and age-70 compulsory-voting thresholds (after the October 2019 general election; n=2,042, ages 16-19 and 67-72) each made 5 choices between two candidates varying in positions on the deficit, IMF loans and abortion, experience, family, gender, favorite music and favorite food.
Reference: Singh, S. P. (2022). Does compulsory voting affect how voters choose? A test using a combined conjoint and regression discontinuity analysis. Comparative Political Studies, 55(12), 2119-2143.
Notes: data/conjoint/singh_2022.R. Level text is the English codebook/value labels (Spanish display text not deposited); whether 'No Opinion'/'No Information'/'No Favorite...' levels were shown as text is undocumented. choice = 1 voted for the candidate (the codebook states the reverse; data and analysis agree with 1 = chosen). Day counts past ages 18/70 (exact birth date) dropped; cov_age is completed years computed from them. Sample includes 16-17-year-olds. Article not read.

Description: UK Prolific respondents aged 18-40 (July 2023) chose between two online-dating profiles (photo plus text) varying on 8 binary attributes: party, political tolerance, ideology, race, education, diet, attractiveness, height. 2,993 respondents, 16 fixed D-optimal choice sets each (female or male profiles by orientation); forced choice.
Reference: Sleiman, Y., Melios, G., & Dolan, P. (2025). "Sleeping with the enemy": Partisanship and tolerance in online dating. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: data/conjoint/sleiman_2025.R. Same 16 choice sets for every respondent (fixed D-optimal design); task = choice-set number, the display order was randomized and not recorded. Attribute levels per set come from the authors' 2.reshape.do; race and attractiveness were shown only by the photo (authors' coding). Profile gender (trial_profile_gender) follows the respondent's orientation. A second deposit of the same paper exists (doi:10.7910/DVN/8HAWA3).

Description: UK respondents (n = 2,518) made 5 choices between two hypothetical parliamentary candidates varying in gender, experience, occupation, children, ethnicity, party, Brexit position and localness, and rated each candidate 0-10.
Reference: Tirado Castro, A., & Banducci, S. (2026). Not just women for women: How gendered affinities affect candidate support. Research & Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/tiradocastro_2026.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (one chosen per pair, checked). Level text from the codebook value descriptions. Codebook says only the chosen candidate was rated, but all profiles carry ratings (kept). Wording paraphrased.

Description: Israeli online respondents (n = 1,170) each compared 8 pairs of proposed public policies (2 per domain: safety, health, welfare, morals) varying on 5 attributes (coercion level of the policy tool, public support, effectiveness, promoter, implementation date); outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Treger, C. (2025). Changing the lens: The contingency of results from conjoint experiments on the outcome variable and the estimand. Research & Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/treger_2025.R. Attribute text is the English Stata value-label text (displayed in Hebrew); actual policy wording not deposited. 69 respondents flagged low quality by the author kept with cov_low_quality=1. Outcome wording not in deposit.

Description: US online respondents (n = 1,570) each compared 8 pairs of proposed public policies (2 per domain: safety, health, welfare, morals) varying on 5 attributes (coercion level of the policy tool, public support, effectiveness, promoter, implementation date); outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Treger, C. (2025). Changing the lens: The contingency of results from conjoint experiments on the outcome variable and the estimand. Research & Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/treger_2025.R. Attribute text is the English Stata value-label text; actual policy wording not deposited. 200 respondents flagged low quality by the author kept with cov_low_quality=1. Outcome wording not in deposit.

Description: YouGov respondents in 11 Middle East and North Africa countries (n = 14,466; 12,025 Sunni analysed in the paper) compared 2 pairs of hypothetical Muslim preachers on 9 attributes, choosing whom they would trust more on religious matters and whose sermon they would listen to, and rating trust in each (0-4).
Reference: Williamson, S., Yildirim, A. K., Grewal, S., & Kuenkler, M. (2023). Preaching politics: How politicization undermines religious authority in the Middle East. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 555-574.
Notes: data/conjoint/williamson_2023.R. Countries pooled (cov_country). All sects kept; the paper analyses Sunni + Salafi only (cov_sect). Attribute text is the authors' English labels; home-country nationality stored as the respondent's country of residence.

Description: 1,979 US Lucid respondents (August 2022) guessed which world region (Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, Middle East) each of 20 hypothetical immigrants came from; profiles varied age, gender, education, English proficiency, prior trips to the U.S., government benefits and police record. The five-option answer is stored as five 0/1 columns.
Reference: Zhirkov, K. (2025). Americans' perceptions about immigrants from different world regions: Evidence from a multinomial conjoint experiment. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 13(2), 192-202.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zhirkov_2025_world_regions.R. Single-profile classification (multinomial outcome) stored as five mutually exclusive 0/1 ratings, one per region option; exactly one is 1 per row. 12 unanswered profiles omitted. Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded.
